results.title: nextflow-io/language-server — the official Nextflow language server (standalone JAR)
results.snippet: The single most actionable Windows-headless finding: the Nextflow LSP is published as a self-contained `language-server-all.jar` on the releases page and is driven over stdio with `java -jar path/to/language-server-all.jar`. Requires only Java 17+, which installs natively on Windows 11 — no WSL distro, no Docker, no VS Code. This means bio-stack can get semantic diagnostics, symbol navigation and config-schema validation for `.nf`/`nextflow.config` files even though the `nextflow` runtime itself cannot run on native Windows. Versioning tracks Nextflow stable releases (v24.10.0-style tags), so it is actively maintained by Seqera. Pairs directly with Claude Code's native LSP client — register it as a custom LSP server command rather than installing the VS Code extension.

results.title: Using an R language server with Claude Code — Christopher T. Kenny (March 2026)
results.snippet: The only source found that gives end-to-end, Windows-explicit Claude Code LSP wiring. Confirms LSP is opt-in via `{"env": {"ENABLE_LSP_TOOL": "1"}}` in settings.json, and names the Windows path explicitly: `C:/Users/<username>/.claude/settings.json`. Shows the plugin-marketplace route (`claude plugin marketplace add christopherkenny/skills` then `claude plugin install r-lsp@christopherkenny/skills`) and the verification method — checking debug logs for "LSP server plugin:r-lsp:r initialized" / "LSP server instance started". Also documents the key behavioral point for an agent stack: the server runs passively, analyzing files and emitting diagnostics without the agent explicitly invoking it. This is the template for registering the Nextflow JAR, basedpyright, and any other LSP in bio-stack, and it closes the R/Bioconductor gap (`install.packages('languageserver')` is native-Windows-installable, unlike Bioconductor CLI workflows).

results.title: astral-sh/ruff-lsp — deprecated in favor of the built-in `ruff server`
results.snippet: Flags an unmaintained tool bio-stack should NOT adopt: ruff-lsp is superseded by `ruff server`, the Rust-native LSP built into the Ruff binary (stable since Ruff v0.5.3, multi-threaded lock-free architecture modeled on rust-analyzer). Since bio-stack already has ruff in its uv/.venv, the language server is zero additional install — just `ruff server` over stdio, fully native on Windows. Also clarifies the division of labor: Ruff covers lint diagnostics and code-action fixes only, and must be paired with a type-checking LSP (basedpyright or Astral's `ty`) for go-to-definition, references and type errors. Relevant to the existing PostToolUse ruff lint gate: an LSP gives the agent diagnostics *before* a write, not just after.

results.title: Setting up a Nextflow environment on Windows 10 — Seqera
results.snippet: Vendor-authored confirmation of the hard host constraint: Nextflow has no native Windows build and requires WSL with an actual Linux distribution installed — the docker-desktop WSL kernel alone is not sufficient, since Nextflow's launcher is a POSIX shell script and its executors assume a Unix filesystem. Corroborated by the official environment-setup docs, which instruct Windows users to install and configure WSL first. Practical consequence for bio-stack: the `wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04` step named in CLAUDE.md is a genuine prerequisite, not optional polish, for anything in the pipeline-engineer lane. The mitigation is the split noted above — run the language server natively on Windows for authoring/validation, and defer execution to WSL or containers.

results.title: Bioconda recipe: samtools — platform availability (linux-64 / osx-64 only)
results.snippet: Evidence for the missing-CLI gap: samtools/bcftools/htslib are distributed for linux-64 and osx-64 only; there is no win-64 conda package, which is why every install guide routes Windows users through WSL Ubuntu. Confirms the CLAUDE.md claim that samtools/bcftools/pysam need WSL2, and by extension that the 'filter VCF/BAM before reading' context-economy rule cannot be executed on native Windows today. Two viable workarounds for the current host: (a) run htslib tools inside a Docker Desktop container (available now, no distro needed) via a thin PowerShell wrapper so the agent's Bash calls still work, or (b) install the Ubuntu distro. Option (a) is the lower-friction path given Docker Desktop is already present.

results.title: snakemake/snakefmt — Snakemake formatter, pip/conda installable and cross-platform
results.snippet: The realistic Snakemake-side tooling for a Windows host: snakefmt is a pure-Python, Black-derived formatter installable with `pip install snakefmt` (or bioconda), and the editor-integration docs explicitly document the Windows executable path pattern (`where snakefmt` → `...\Python\Scripts\snakefmt.exe`), so it runs headlessly from the agent on native Windows. Useful as a PostToolUse formatting gate for `.smk`/Snakefile writes alongside the existing ruff gate. Caveat worth flagging: a true `snakemake-language-server` with documented stdio config did not surface in these results — the VS Code Snakefmt extension bundles a formatting-only server, so Snakemake gets formatting and Python-level linting but not the semantic LSP coverage that Nextflow gets from its official JAR. If the choice of workflow engine is still open, that asymmetry argues for Nextflow/nf-core.

results.title: BixBench: a Comprehensive Benchmark for LLM-based Agents in Computational Biology (FutureHouse, arXiv:2503.00096)
results.snippet: The single most load-bearing counterweight to tool accumulation. 53 real-world bioinformatics scenarios / ~296 open-answer questions in reproducible Dockerized Jupyter capsules; frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) reach only ~17% accuracy open-answer and no better than random on multiple choice. Named failure classes map directly onto guardrail design: (a) failure at long multi-step analytical trajectories — argues for checkpointing, SubagentStop verification and narrow per-subagent scope rather than one mega-agent; (b) poor interpretation of generated plots — argues against trusting agent-authored figure narration and for numeric assertions (test statistics, n, effect sizes) written to disk alongside every figure; (c) reliance on rote knowledge instead of actually running the computation — the direct evidence for a PostToolUse hook that refuses a claimed result with no corresponding entry in runs/provenance.jsonl. Also the correct choice if bio-stack wants a local eval harness: the repo (github.com/Future-House/BixBench) ships the capsules and agent scaffold, and its Docker-based environment runs on Docker Desktop without a WSL2 distro.

results.title: GenoTEX: An LLM Agent Benchmark for Automated Gene Expression Data Analysis (MLCB 2025 Oral; github.com/Liu-Hy/GenoTEX)
results.snippet: The most directly applicable benchmark to the omics-analyst subagent, and the best-documented source of *statistical* failure modes. Expert-curated, structured as three separately scored stages — dataset selection, preprocessing, statistical analysis — with reference code and reference results, so it localizes where an agent breaks rather than reporting one aggregate score. Reported failures include errors extracting the data matrix and incorrect parameters passed to regression models, with cumulative error risk across the pipeline dominating end-to-end performance; a persistent gap versus human experts concentrates in tasks needing domain knowledge and clinical-metadata interpretation (i.e. covariate and batch handling, exactly where a silent wrong answer looks plausible). Concrete implications for bio-stack: stage-gate the DEG pipeline instead of running it end-to-end, and add hooks asserting the non-negotiables GenoTEX scores — declared design matrix/covariates, explicit multiple-testing correction method, and fixed random_state — since these are precisely what agents omit without erroring.

results.title: LAB-Bench: Measuring Capabilities of Language Models for Biology Research (FutureHouse, arXiv:2407.10362)
results.snippet: The capability-level complement to BixBench: 2,400+ MCQs partitioned into DbQA (database retrieval), LitQA2 (literature), SeqQA (DNA/protein sequence manipulation), FigQA, TableQA, ProtocolQA and SuppQA. Useful here as a *routing* argument rather than a tool list — the per-subtask breakdown is evidence that database lookup and sequence manipulation are separable, individually measurable competencies, supporting bio-stack's existing rule that lookups go to gget/biocontext instead of model recall, and that seq-designer's sequence edits need deterministic verification. ProtocolQA is the relevant precedent for auto-generated methods sections: it measures whether a model can detect a flawed protocol, which is the check /metodos needs before it converts provenance into prose. Note 20% of the set is withheld as a private test split specifically to detect training contamination — a caution against citing headline LAB-Bench scores from model cards as evidence of fitness. Public subset: huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench.

results.title: Large language model agents for biological intelligence across genomics, proteomics, spatial biology, and biomedicine (Briefings in Bioinformatics, 2026)
results.snippet: The most current (March 2026) comparative assessment of bio agents, and the one that names reproducibility as a first-class failure axis rather than an afterthought. Reports consistent cross-system challenges — unstable reasoning, limited biological grounding, retrieval misalignment, and explicit barriers to reproducibility and biosafety — across genomics, proteomics, spatial biology and biomedicine agents. 'Retrieval misalignment' is the direct evidence for guarding the nvidia-nemo RAG path (grounding checks / rerank thresholds, refusing to answer from low-scoring passages); 'unstable reasoning' is the argument for seeded, scripted analysis over ad-hoc terminal commands, which bio-stack already mandates but does not yet enforce. Its framing of biosafety alongside reproducibility also supports keeping the CLAUDE.md risk-agent referral rule as an enforced hook rather than a prose convention.

results.title: The rise and potential opportunities of large language model agents in bioinformatics and biomedicine (Briefings in Bioinformatics, 26(6), bbaf601, 2025)
results.snippet: Survey-level grounding for the architecture choices in bio-stack, with a challenges section that enumerates hallucination and interpretability, timeliness of knowledge updates, data privacy, and framework interaction/extension. Its review of existing systems is useful as prior art for what to build versus adopt: BioMaster (multi-agent workflow automation with RAG-backed domain retrieval plus a dedicated debug agent doing iterative error correction) and CellAgent (scRNA-seq processing with dual-layer memory and self-iterative optimization) are the closest published analogues to pipeline-engineer and omics-analyst respectively, and both converge on an explicit self-correction/verification agent as a separate role — evidence that a verification subagent or Stop-hook reviewer is a recognized pattern, not an invention. 'Timeliness of knowledge updates' is the survey's name for silent version drift: model-internal knowledge of tool flags and database schemas goes stale, which is the argument for always resolving parameters from live MCP/DB lookups rather than recall.

results.title: The Hidden Cost of Reproducibility: Commercial Software Dependency in Published Research and the Version Accessibility Gap (EPJ Research Infrastructures, 2026)
results.snippet: Quantitative evidence for the version-pinning guardrail, from the literature rather than from agent benchmarks. Across 2,922 articles with detected software use, only 17.0% of detected software tools carried a version number, and 63.4% depended on at least one commercial tool whose cited versions were largely classified as no longer obtainable from the vendor. Read against bio-stack: an auto-generated Methods section that names tools without versions reproduces the exact defect this paper measures, so /metodos should be blocked from emitting a tool name unless runs/provenance.jsonl carries its resolved version — meaning the provenance hook must capture versions (uv.lock hashes, container digests, NIM model slug plus endpoint revision) at call time, since NIM slugs change server-side and cannot be reconstructed after the fact. Related evidence in the same search space: ~50% of surveyed bioinformatics tools were hard to install or reproduce due to undocumented dependencies, and GigaScience's workflow reproducibility scale (doi:10.1093/gigascience/giad031) proposes automatic validation that biological *interpretation* — not just file checksums — is preserved across reruns, which is the stronger test a Stop hook could implement.

claims.claim: LAB-Bench's reported frontier-model scores are a no-tool floor, not a measure of agent capability: the authors evaluated Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Llama 3 with no tools or internet access, while human expert comparators were allowed tools — and they explicitly predict that tool augmentation will rapidly close the gap. This is direct published justification for prioritizing database/compute MCP servers over prompt engineering in an agent stack.
claims.quote: Importantly, none of the models evaluated here were augmented with any tools, including internet use. ... We expect that efforts to provide models with access to relevant tools will rapidly improve performance on several of the benchmarks here.

claims.claim: On the hardest multi-step molecular-biology tasks (CloningScenarios, 41 questions; best model ~28% vs 60% for humans), models reach above-random scores by eliminating implausible distractors and guessing rather than by reasoning correctly — meaning an agent must not be trusted to do cloning/construct design by LLM reasoning alone, and deterministic tooling (biopython, restriction-site mapping, primer design) must be in the loop.
claims.quote: Even when models answer questions correctly, it is clear they are only able answer correctly by using heuristics to eliminate unlikely distractors and then guess.

claims.claim: The largest single subtask block in LAB-Bench (DbQA, 650 questions across 10 subtasks) is defined as requiring retrieval from specific standard biology databases, and no evaluated model performed well on it — evidence that database-access MCP servers (UniProt, Ensembl, NCBI/Entrez, PDB, etc.) target a measured, named capability gap rather than a speculative one.
claims.quote: DbQA questions are intended to require the access and retrieval of information from specific common databases used in biology research.

claims.claim: Sequence-manipulation failures (SeqQA, 750 questions across 15 subtasks; models ~45% vs ~88% human) are attributed to the models' inability to handle long strings, particularly extracting subsequences and mapping internal restriction digests — so sequence work in an agent stack should be delegated to executed code/CLI tools, never done in-context.
claims.quote: notoriously poor at manipulating long strings

claims.claim: LAB-Bench separates accuracy (correct/all) from precision (correct/attempted) and offers an explicit decline-to-answer option; models' willingness to answer varied widely and tracked whether a question required lookup, with refusal on lookup-heavy categories (LitQA2, SuppQA) pushing accuracy below random. This supports building abstention/coverage reporting into an agent's scientific-correctness guardrails rather than reporting a single accuracy figure.
claims.quote: Models displayed a widely varying willingness to answer questions across categories, roughly corresponding to lower coverage on question types explicitly requiring lookup.

claims.claim: GenoTEX is an expert-curated, publicly released benchmark (github.com/Liu-Hy/GenoTEX) of 1,384 gene-trait association problems spanning 911 gene-expression datasets and 152,415 samples, annotated by nine bioinformaticians over ~20 weeks — i.e. a concrete, runnable evaluation suite an omics agent stack can be scored against rather than a qualitative claim of competence.
claims.quote: Total problems: 1384; Datasets: 911; Total samples: 152,415

claims.claim: State-of-the-art multi-agent LLM pipelines remain materially worse than human bioinformaticians at end-to-end gene-trait association analysis: GenoAgent reaches 0.74 AUROC versus 0.89 for expert humans (with ~43% precision / ~50% recall / 41% F1 on identified genes), so autonomous agent output on differential-expression-style tasks must not be treated as publication-grade without expert review.
claims.quote: GenoAgent achieved an AUROC score of 0.74...a significant gap remains compared to human expert performance (0.89 AUROC).

claims.claim: The dominant failure mode is not statistics but metadata/phenotype curation: agents score a Composite Similarity Correlation of 80.63% on gene-matrix preprocessing but only 32.28% on trait (clinical feature) extraction, which localizes the guardrail to sample-annotation / cohort-definition steps (the exact point where a provenance hook or human-in-the-loop checkpoint pays off).
claims.quote: preprocessing trait data proved considerably more challenging...with a significantly lower CSC score of 32.28%

claims.claim: When handed data already preprocessed by human bioinformaticians, agent statistical analysis is near-expert (94.81% precision, 92.27% recall, 0.97 AUROC), meaning the bottleneck in LLM-driven omics is upstream data curation rather than the modelling/statistics step — an argument for spending agent-stack effort on curated data ingestion and provenance rather than on statistical automation.
claims.quote: we provided datasets preprocessed by human bioinformaticians...several agent-based methods [achieved] good performance

claims.claim: LLM self-correction loops degrade rather than converge: additional review rounds yield diminishing returns and the reviewing agent emits inconsistent feedback containing technical errors — evidence that deterministic gates (linters, schema/type checks, unit tests, PostToolUse hooks) should backstop LLM code-review subagents rather than being replaced by them.
claims.quote: additional rounds yield diminishing returns

claims.claim: ToolUniverse (Zitnik Lab, Harvard Medical School) ships a first-party Model Context Protocol server, so a single MCP endpoint can expose its entire scientific tool catalog to an agent over the network; it installs as a pure-Python package (`pip install tooluniverse`, repo https://github.com/mims-harvard/ToolUniverse, site https://aiscientist.tools) with no GPU or Linux requirement, making it installable on the bio-stack's Windows 11 / Python 3.11 uv venv. The paper documents explicit Claude Desktop config (Settings -> Developer -> Edit Config, command `tooluniverse-mcp-claude`) and Gemini CLI usage, i.e. it is model-agnostic MCP client integration.
claims.quote: ToolUniverse also implements the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows all operations like searching and invoking tools to be communicated with the ToolUniverse server over a network.

claims.claim: ToolUniverse federates more than 600 tools in one server, broken down in the paper as ~281 APIs, ~164 scientific software packages, ~84 databases, ~38 agents, ~17 ML models, ~6 human-expert-feedback tools, ~4 embedding stores and 1 robotics tool, with named sources including FDA, PubChem, OpenTargets, DrugBank and Human Protein Atlas. This is an order of magnitude more tools than any single MCP server already in the bio-stack (gget-mcp, biocontext_kb, biomcp), but it overlaps heavily with Open Targets/ChEMBL/PubChem coverage the stack already has, so it is an additive consolidation candidate rather than a pure gap-filler.
claims.quote: ToolUniverse integrates more than 600 tools that span machine learning models, agents, software utilities, robotics, databases, and APIs.

claims.claim: Because 600+ tool specifications cannot all be held in an agent's context, ToolUniverse separates discovery from execution into two operations — 'Find Tool' (natural language -> tool specification) and 'Call Tool' — with the Tool Finder using three complementary retrieval strategies (keyword search, LLM-based in-context search, embedding search). This is the token-efficiency mechanism a large-catalog MCP server needs, and the paper explicitly flags that the LLM in-context search variant is bounded by the model's finite context window.
claims.quote: By combining speed, precision, and depth, AI scientist systems can locate tools to execute user tasks.

claims.claim: ToolUniverse claims a documented, multi-stage tool-reliability process rather than ad-hoc API wrapping — test-example sampling, expert human review, and automated optimization — plus structured bug reporting and regular maintenance, with tools drawn from peer-reviewed and regulatory sources. This is the kind of maintenance/QA evidence the research question asks for when comparing bio MCP servers, though it is the authors' own self-report in a preprint, not third-party audit.
claims.quote: We established the reliability of tools in ToolUniverse through a multi-step process that combines test example sampling, expert human review, and automated optimization.

claims.claim: ToolUniverse includes agentic meta-tools that let the agent extend its own toolset at runtime: Tool Discover synthesizes new tool specifications and executable implementations from natural-language descriptions with validation and iterative refinement, and Tool Optimizer refines existing tool specifications over test-case/analyze/feedback cycles (default max 3 rounds). This is directly relevant to the 'maximally autonomous' goal — an agent that can author and repair its own MCP tool definitions — but also a provenance risk, since auto-generated tools are not covered by the human expert review path.
claims.quote: Tool Discover generates new tools from natural language descriptions. It synthesizes formal specifications, produces executable implementations, validates outputs, and iteratively refines quality.

results.title: Plugins reference — Claude Code Docs (Anthropic official)
results.snippet: The single highest-value page for this angle: it defines the full plugin surface a bio-stack could be packaged into — skills/, agents/, hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, AND .lsp.json — plus the fact that .claude-plugin/plugin.json is now optional (components auto-discovered in default locations). Two things materially change what this stack can adopt: (1) native LSP client config lives in `lspServers`/.lsp.json as `{"<name>": {"command", "args", "extensionToLanguage": {".py": "python"}}}` with optional `transport`, `env`, `initializationOptions`, `settings`, `startupTimeout`, `shutdownTimeout`, `restartOnCrash`, `maxRestarts`, and `diagnostics` (default true — pushes diagnostics into context, which is exactly the ruff/basedpyright gate the stack currently fakes with a PostToolUse hook). Critically, the language server binary must be installed separately; the plugin only wires the connection. Extension collisions matter: if two enabled LSP servers claim the same extension, the first registered wins and the rest never start — so a python-lsp plugin plus a local basedpyright entry would silently conflict. (2) The hook event list is far larger than the four events this stack uses: 28+ events including SubagentStart/SubagentStop, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, PermissionRequest/PermissionDenied, TaskCreated/TaskCompleted, InstructionsLoaded, FileChanged, CwdChanged, WorktreeCreate/Remove, PreCompact/PostCompact, PreModelSwitch/PostModelSwitch, Elicitation/ElicitationResult, Setup, and SessionEnd. Also names a new `monitors/monitors.json` component (background processes piping stdout to Claude as notifications, interactive CLI only) — a plausible home for long-running NIM job polling. Pins version floors: v2.1.205+ for `restartOnCrash`/`shutdownTimeout`, v2.1.207+ for user-config restrictions, v2.1.218+ for extended boolean frontmatter.

results.title: Hooks reference — Claude Code Docs (Anthropic official)
results.snippet: Authoritative hook contract, and it shows the bio-stack's four Python `command` hooks are one of five handler types. The others are directly useful for scientific rigor: `prompt` hooks (single-turn model evaluation, e.g. "does this analysis declare a seed and a multiple-testing correction?", default 30s timeout, `model` selectable), `agent` hooks (experimental; spawn a subagent with Read/Grep/Glob to verify a condition), `mcp_tool` hooks (call a connected MCP tool as the hook body — note: unavailable at SessionStart/Setup because there is no MCP client yet, which affects the existing SessionStart env report if it were ever rewritten), and `http`. Exit-code semantics are the load-bearing part for a data/raw guard: exit 2 blocks and ALWAYS wins, even if the JSON says `permissionDecision: "allow"`; exit 0 with JSON on stdout drives `permissionDecision` (allow/deny/request_confirmation), `permissionDecisionReason`, `updatedInput` (rewrite tool input in flight), `additionalContext`, and `systemMessage`. Plain stdout is injected as visible context only for UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, SessionStart and PostModelSwitch — for every other event it goes to the debug log only, which is a common silent failure. Also: `if` permission-rule filters (`"if": "Bash(rm *)"`, `"Edit(*.ts)"`) let a guard fire narrowly instead of on every Bash call; `async`/`asyncRewake` for non-blocking hooks; `once: true` (skill frontmatter only); `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` placeholders; `"shell": "powershell"` to force PowerShell, which matters on this Windows host. SessionStart matchers are startup|resume|clear|compact|fork. Hook input now carries `scratchpad_dir` (v2.1.257+) and `prompt_id` (v2.1.196+); matcher niceties need v2.1.191+/v2.1.195+.

results.title: Extend Claude with skills (SKILL.md authoring) — Claude Code Docs
results.snippet: Official SKILL.md contract, and the token-efficiency argument for migrating the bio-stack's five slash commands and much of CLAUDE.md into skills: skill bodies load only when invoked, so large reference material (NIM slug tables, nf-core conventions, ACMG criteria) costs nothing until needed — unlike CLAUDE.md, which is always resident. Frontmatter that maps onto this stack's gaps: `context: fork` + `agent: <type>` runs a skill in an isolated subagent that does NOT see conversation history (background by default; `background: false` to wait — v2.1.218+), which is the right shape for /metodos-style log mining and for keeping huge biological file output out of the main context; `disable-model-invocation: true` for side-effectful commands (a NIM submission or a data/raw write should never be model-triggered); `user-invocable: false` for pure background knowledge; `allowed-tools` to pre-approve narrowly (`Bash(git *) Read`), noting permissions clear at the end of the invocation turn; `paths` globs to gate activation; `model`/`effort` overrides; `arguments` for named `$name` substitution (string form v2.1.199+). Dynamic context injection is notable for a provenance stack: `!` + backtick shell commands (or a fenced ```! block) execute BEFORE Claude sees the skill and their stdout is substituted inline — so a skill can embed `git status`, `nvidia-smi`, or a tail of runs/provenance.jsonl deterministically rather than asking the model to go read it. Substitutions include `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`, `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` (v2.1.196+), `${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}`. Guidance: keep SKILL.md under ~500 lines and push detail into sibling files referenced by relative link (progressive disclosure); combine with hooks when a skill's behavior must be enforced deterministically rather than suggested.

results.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP — Claude Code Docs
results.snippet: Directly addresses the token-efficiency half of the question for a stack running ~15 MCP servers. MCP tool output has a 10,000-token warning threshold and a 25,000-token hard limit by default; over-limit output is written to a file under ~/.claude/projects/tool-results/ and replaced in-context by a file reference — which is the same pattern the stack's nvidia-bio tools already implement by hand, and `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` raises it globally. Per-tool overrides are possible server-side via `_meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"]`, useful when writing the custom nvidia-bio/nvidia-nemo servers. Also documents: four transports (http recommended for remote, stdio local, sse deprecated, ws), the three scopes (local in ~/.claude.json, project in a committed .mcp.json, user), `${VAR}`/`${VAR:-default}` env expansion and `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`/`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` placeholders inside .mcp.json, the plugin tool-name shape `mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>__<tool>` used in permission allowlists (essential for trimming prompts on this stack's large tool surface), `headersHelper` for dynamic auth (a fit for rotating NVIDIA API keys), timeout knobs (`MCP_TIMEOUT` startup, `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT`, `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_TOOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT`), `list_changed` dynamic tool refresh, and auto-backgrounding of MCP calls over ~2 min (v2.1.212+, `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_AUTO_BACKGROUND_MS`) — relevant to long NIM folds. Caveat for this angle: the page does NOT document MCP resources (@server:resource) or MCP prompts-as-slash-commands, so treat those as unconfirmed rather than assumed. Windows note: `claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop` is macOS/WSL only, and desktop-app WSL sessions do not support claude.ai connectors.

results.title: Run Claude Code programmatically (headless mode) — Claude Code Docs
results.snippet: The official basis for turning bio-stack analyses into unattended, reproducible runs — the thing an academic pipeline needs for overnight NIM batches and re-running an analysis to prove it reproduces. `claude -p/--print` executes one prompt non-interactively and exits, still saving a resumable session unless `--no-session-persistence` is passed; `--output-format json` (and `stream-json`) gives machine-parseable results you can pipe into runs/provenance.jsonl instead of scraping terminal text. Key flag for scheduled jobs with nobody at the keyboard: `--permission-prompts none`. Ties into the Agent SDK (Python and TypeScript packages exposing the same agent loop, tools and context management, plus the CLI-as-subprocess pattern), and to routines/cloud scheduling for cron-style or event-triggered runs. Note for this angle: the `Setup` hook event fires specifically during `--init-only` / `-p` initialization, and settings-file hooks still run in untrusted folders under `-p` while project skill/subagent frontmatter hooks are skipped unless the folder is trusted — a real constraint if the stack's guards are moved into frontmatter rather than settings.json.

results.title: anthropics/claude-plugins-official — Anthropic-managed plugin marketplace
results.snippet: The first-party marketplace to check before installing community plugins, and the distribution channel for LSP plugins (typescript-lsp and similar) that the plugins-reference describes. Install path is `/plugin install <name>@claude-plugins-official`, or `/plugin > Discover` to browse; the repo splits `/plugins` (Anthropic-developed) from `/external_plugins` (partner/community), which is the cleanest available maintenance signal — an Anthropic-managed entry is the safer default for an academic stack than an unvetted Smithery/PulseMCP listing. Caveat worth flagging: the repo landing page does not enumerate plugin names inline, so the concrete list (and whether a Python LSP plugin exists versus needing a hand-written .lsp.json pointing at the already-installed basedpyright) has to be confirmed in `/plugin > Discover` or by browsing the directories. Since LSP plugins never ship the server binary, any Nextflow/R/Snakemake language server would still need its own install — and on this host those are WSL2-side tools, so a distro install is a prerequisite regardless of plugin availability.

claims.claim: Claude Code enforces MCP tool-output token limits: it warns above 10,000 tokens and caps output at a default maximum of 25,000 tokens, raisable via the MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS environment variable. This is the concrete knob for [REDACTED] when adding high-volume bioinformatics MCP servers (UniProt/PDB/Ensembl/Entrez wrappers) to the bio-stack.
claims.quote: Claude Code displays a warning when any MCP tool output exceeds 10,000 tokens ... the default maximum is 25,000 tokens ... To increase the limit for tools that produce large outputs: `export MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS=50000`

claims.claim: When a non-image MCP tool result exceeds the output limit, Claude Code automatically spills it to a file in the session's `tool-results` directory under `~/.claude/projects/` and replaces the inline result with the file path, so the model reads it only on demand. This is a native harness-level implementation of the bio-stack's 'write to runs/, return only the path' convention, meaning third-party bio MCP servers that dump large FASTA/mmCIF/VCF payloads are partially mitigated without custom code.
claims.quote: when a result with no image content exceeds the limit, Claude Code saves it to a file and replaces it in the conversation with a message that names the file path, so Claude reads the file when it needs the content. The file goes in the session's `tool-results` directory under `~/.claude/projects/`

claims.claim: MCP servers can be installed at project scope, which stores the configuration in a `.mcp.json` file in the project root that is shareable via version control — the mechanism for making the bio-stack's MCP server set reproducible and committable once `git init` is run.
claims.quote: claude mcp add --transport http shared-server --scope project https://example.com/mcp

claims.claim: Per-server `timeout` in `.mcp.json` is a hard wall-clock limit per tool call that server progress notifications cannot extend, and an idle timeout aborts calls with no response/progress after 5 minutes (HTTP/SSE/WebSocket) or 30 minutes (stdio) — configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_TOOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT. This directly constrains long-running hosted NIM calls (AlphaFold2/Boltz/MSA search) made through the custom nvidia-bio server.
claims.quote: The per-server `timeout` is a hard wall-clock limit per tool call, and progress notifications from the server don't extend it. Values below 1000 are ignored and fall through to `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT`, or to its default of about 28 hours when that variable is unset.

claims.claim: An MCP server can annotate an individual tool with `anthropic/maxResultSizeChars` in its `_meta` block to raise that tool's output threshold, up to a hard ceiling of 500,000 characters — an authoring-side lever for the bio-stack's own nvidia-bio/nvidia-nemo servers to selectively allow large schema or RAG payloads without globally raising MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS.
claims.quote: Claude Code raises that tool's threshold to the annotated value, up to a hard ceiling of 500,000 characters.

claims.claim: Claude Code skills implement progressive disclosure: only the skill's name/description metadata is always in context, while the body loads on invocation — making bundled reference material effectively free until needed. The description + when_to_use pair is capped at 1,536 characters, and Anthropic recommends keeping SKILL.md under 500 lines with detail moved to separate referenced files. This is the core token-efficiency mechanism for packaging bioinformatics protocols (e.g. seed-fixing, multiple-testing, methods-section rules) without permanent context cost, unlike CLAUDE.md.
claims.quote: Unlike CLAUDE.md content, a skill's body loads only when it's used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it.

claims.claim: A SKILL.md can declare `context: fork` with an `agent` field (Explore, Plan, general-purpose, or a custom agent) to execute the skill inside a forked subagent context, and `background: false` (Claude Code v2.1.218+) makes the invoking turn wait for the subagent's result instead of backgrounding it. This means an existing subagent roster (structure-bio, omics-analyst, variant-curator, etc.) can be driven from skills rather than only by delegation prose, isolating large bio-file processing from the main context window.
claims.quote: Set to `fork` to run in a forked subagent context.

claims.claim: Skills can register hooks declaratively via a `hooks` YAML object in SKILL.md, and those hooks keep running for the remainder of the session after the skill is invoked. This allows provenance logging, data/raw write guards, or lint gates to be scoped to a specific workflow (attached when the skill runs) rather than being permanently configured in settings.json.
claims.quote: Hooks that Claude Code registers when the skill is invoked and keeps running for the rest of the session.

claims.claim: Skills carry per-invocation permission scoping through `allowed-tools` (tools usable without a permission prompt, with pattern syntax such as `Bash(git add *)`) and `disallowed-tools` (tools removed from Claude's pool while the skill is active); both grants expire at the user's next message rather than persisting. This is the documented mechanism for autonomous unattended runs that still cannot touch specified tools.
claims.quote: Tools Claude can use without asking permission during the turn that invokes this skill. The grant clears when you send your next message.

claims.claim: Skills support deterministic bundled executables and dynamic context injection: `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` resolves to the skill's own directory for invoking bundled scripts (requires Claude Code v2.1.196+), and backtick-bang syntax runs shell commands whose stdout is injected into the skill body at invocation time, with `shell: powershell` selectable instead of the bash default — relevant on a Windows-primary host. An org policy key `disableSkillShellExecution` can turn the shell injection off, and commands are not executed for skills synced from a claude.ai account.

claims.claim: Claude Code's hook surface is far larger than the four events bio-stack currently uses (SessionStart, PreToolUse, PostToolUse): the official reference documents ~30 events including SessionEnd, Stop, StopFailure, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, PreCompact, PostCompact, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, UserPromptSubmit, FileChanged, InstructionsLoaded and Setup — giving concrete unused hooks for provenance flush-on-exit, failed-run logging, and pre-compaction summarization.
claims.quote: Hooks are user-defined shell commands, HTTP endpoints, MCP tool calls, LLM prompts, or subagents that execute automatically at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle.

claims.claim: Hook matchers accept regex over MCP tool names of the form mcp__<server>__<tool>, so a provenance logger can be scoped to e.g. `mcp__nvidia-bio__.*`; but plugin-bundled MCP servers are named mcp__plugin_<plugin-name>_<server-name>__<tool>, and a matcher written against the bare server key will silently never fire — a real failure mode for bio-stack's plugin MCPs (PubMed, bioRxiv, ChEMBL, Open Targets), whose tools are exposed as mcp__plugin_bio-research_*.
claims.quote: A matcher written against the bare server key never fires for these tools.

claims.claim: Exit-code semantics for hooks are counterintuitive and affect the data/raw PreToolUse guard: only exit code 2 blocks an action by exit status alone, while the conventional Unix failure code 1 is treated as a non-blocking error and the tool call proceeds — so a guard script that merely `exit 1`s on a protected path does NOT protect the path.
claims.quote: Without valid JSON on stdout, Claude Code treats exit code 1 as a non-blocking error and proceeds with the action, even though 1 is the conventional Unix failure code.

claims.claim: On Windows (bio-stack's host), shell-form hook commands run under Git Bash by default and PowerShell must be selected explicitly ("shell": "powershell" or by invoking powershell.exe with -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File), and exec-form hooks can only spawn real .exe executables — .cmd/.bat shims (which is how npm/npx/uv-installed tools commonly appear on Windows) cannot be spawned without a shell.
claims.quote: Exec form requires real `.exe` executables

claims.claim: Hooks are not limited to shell commands: the config supports type "command", "http" (URL + headers with an allowedEnvVars allowlist), "mcp_tool" (server + tool + templated input such as ${tool_input.file_path}), "prompt" (LLM call with a model field), and "agent" (subagent), with default timeouts of 600s for command/http/mcp_tool, 30s for prompt and 60s for agent — meaning a reproducibility gate could call an MCP tool or an LLM judge directly rather than shelling out to Python.
claims.quote: Hooks are user-defined shell commands, HTTP endpoints, MCP tool calls, LLM prompts, or subagents that execute automatically at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle.

5. Supporting quote — CONFIRMED verbatim: "By combining speed, precision, and depth, AI scientist systems can locate tools to execute user tasks."

NOT OUTDATED IN SUBSTANCE. Version history: v1 27-Sep-2025, v2 22-Oct-2025, v3 07-Aug-2026 (current). A Chance-Corrected Answer"), was fetched specifically to refute the premise and instead corroborates it — it accepts that accuracy degrades as tool catalogs grow ("LongFuncEval and Rabinovich and Anaby-Tavor show that function-calling accuracy degrades as tool catalogs grow") and treats retrieval depth as an optimization target rather than calling prior degradation results overstated. findings.claim: P0 — The existing PreToolUse guard on data/raw may not actually block anything: in Claude Code, exit code 2 is the only exit status that blocks a tool call, while the conventional Unix failure code 1 is treated as a non-blocking error and the write proceeds. Fix the guard to `exit 2` with a stderr reason, or (preferably) emit JSON on stdout with `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny"` and exit 0, then verify empirically against Write/Edit.
findings.evidence: Official hooks reference, verbatim: "Without valid JSON on stdout, Claude Code treats exit code 1 as a non-blocking error and proceeds with the action, even though 1 is the conventional Unix failure code." The same page: "exit code 2 is the only exit code that blocks through the code alone", and PreToolUse is explicitly listed as a blocking event ("Blocks the tool call" under exit 2; exit 2 blocks whether or not JSON is printed, overriding even a permissionDecision of allow). Independent write-ups converge on the same silent-failure mode. Caveat carried from verification: issue anthropics/claude-code#13744 reports that even exit 2 was at one point unreliable for Write/Edit specifically, so the guard must be tested against an actual attempted write to data/raw rather than assumed correct from the doc. Target file: C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack\.claude\hooks\ (the guard script referenced from .claude/settings.json).

findings.claim: P0 — Windows hook execution semantics are a live foot-gun for this host: shell-form hook commands (no `args`) run under Git Bash when Git Bash is on PATH — which it is here — not PowerShell, so PowerShell syntax in a hook silently fails; exec form (`args` set) can only spawn real .exe files, not .cmd/.bat shims; and `shell: "powershell"` has a known bug where it spawns `pwsh` with no `powershell.exe` fallback. The safe form is explicit invocation: `powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File <script>`.
findings.evidence: Docs: "Shell form passes the string to sh -c on macOS and Linux, Git Bash on Windows, or PowerShell when Git Bash isn't installed"; the `shell` field "Accepts bash or powershell. Defaults to bash"; and "On Windows, exec form requires command to resolve to a real executable such as a .exe" — "The .cmd and .bat shims that npm, npx, eslint, and other tools install ... are not executables and can't be spawned without a shell." Issue #59225 shows the Git-Bash-default biting in the wild (a PowerShell-style hook failing with a bash syntax error); #90077 shows `shell: powershell` spawning pwsh with no powershell.exe fallback. Applies directly: bio-stack's hooks in C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack\.claude\settings.json are all shell form (`uv run --script ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/...`) with no `args` and no `shell` key, so they currently route through Git Bash. Mitigating correction from verification: uv/pip console scripts on Windows ARE real .exe launchers in .venv\Scripts\, and uv itself is uv.exe, so this stack's `uv run` hooks would in fact be exec-form-spawnable — the .cmd-shim hazard applies to npm/npx-installed tools, not to the uv-based hooks.

findings.claim: P0 — A hook matcher scoped to an MCP server must be written as a regex ending in `.*`, and plugin-bundled MCP servers use a different name shape: `mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>__<tool>`. A provenance matcher written as `mcp__nvidia-bio` (no `.*`) or against the bare server key of a plugin MCP silently never fires. bio-stack's plugin MCPs are exposed as `mcp__plugin_bio-research_pubmed__*`, `mcp__plugin_bio-research_chembl__*`, `mcp__plugin_bio-research_ot__*`, `mcp__plugin_bio-research_biorxiv__*`, `mcp__plugin_bio-research_c-trials__*`.
findings.evidence: hooks.md, verbatim: "Tools from a plugin-bundled MCP server use a scoped server segment that includes the plugin name: mcp__plugin_<plugin-name>_<server-name>__<tool>. A matcher written against the bare server key never fires for these tools." Also: MCP tools follow `mcp__<server>__<tool>`; matchers are tested with JavaScript's RegExp.prototype.test; and a bare `mcp__memory` containing only exact-match characters is compared as an exact string and matches nothing — the `.*` suffix is mandatory. Cross-confirmed on /docs/en/mcp: "Use this full name when referencing the tool in permission rules ... or a hook matcher." Status for bio-stack: the hazard is prospective, not active — the current provenance hook uses `matcher: "*"` and therefore does fire on everything, including plugin MCPs. It bites the moment the logger is narrowed to per-server matchers, which is the usual next refactor.

findings.claim: P1 — The provenance log is structurally incomplete and Claude Code already ships the events to fix it. The official hooks reference documents ~30 lifecycle events (five handler types: `command`, `http`, `mcp_tool`, `prompt`, `agent`), of which bio-stack uses three. Three concrete additions: `PostToolUseFailure` (fires after a tool call fails — today's PostToolUse logger only fires on success, so failed NIM calls and crashed scripts are invisible in runs/provenance.jsonl, which silently biases the auto-generated Methods section); `SessionEnd` (flush/finalize a run); `PreCompact` (summarize or back up the transcript before context compaction).
findings.evidence: Both official pages enumerate the same event set (33 events on the plugins-reference table): SessionStart, Setup, UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, Notification, MessageDisplay, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted, Stop, StopFailure, TeammateIdle, InstructionsLoaded, ConfigChange, CwdChanged, DirectoryAdded, FileChanged, WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove, PreCompact, PostCompact, PreModelSwitch, PostModelSwitch, Elicitation, ElicitationResult, SessionEnd. Handler types verbatim: command / http / mcp_tool / prompt / agent. Local CLI is 2.1.270, well past any version gate. Two caveats: the narrower plugins/plugin-dev hook-development SKILL.md lists only 9 events — read /docs/en/hooks, not that skill, for the full surface; and at least one secondary source describes the `agent` handler type as experimental.

findings.claim: P1 — Skills (SKILL.md), not CLAUDE.md, are the right container for scientific-rigor protocols (seed fixing, multiple-testing correction, effect-size reporting, figure/axis conventions, Methods-section rules). Only name/description metadata sits permanently in context; the body loads on invocation — "long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it." Author to ≤500 lines with detail in referenced files, and keep `description` ≤1,024 characters if the skill is ever to be published (the 1,536-char figure is the combined description+when_to_use listing truncation, not the spec's hard limit).
findings.evidence: Official skills docs, verbatim: "Unlike CLAUDE.md content, a skill's body loads only when it's used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it"; "the combined description and when_to_use text is truncated at 1,536 characters in the skill listing to reduce context usage"; "Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material to separate files." `when_to_use` is a real documented frontmatter field. Three qualifications from verification: (a) once invoked, the rendered SKILL.md enters the conversation as a single message and stays there across later turns — "free" holds only up to first invocation; (b) the Agent Skills spec enforces a stricter 1,024-char limit on `description` alone (anthropics/skills issues #1613/#1622 flag shipped skills at 1,068-1,077 chars as over-limit), so conflating the two is a real authoring error for publishable skills; (c) third-party reports of a `skillListingMaxDescChars` override in settings.json are undocumented and unverified. Split vote reflects that the mechanism is well-documented but the "unlike CLAUDE.md" framing understates post-invocation persistence.

findings.claim: P1 — The existing subagent roster can be driven declaratively from skills instead of delegation prose: SKILL.md supports `context: fork` plus an `agent:` field naming a custom subagent from `.claude/agents/` (bio-stack has structure-bio, omics-analyst, seq-designer, variant-curator, pipeline-engineer, lit-scout there), and `background: false` (Claude Code v2.1.218+; local install is 2.1.270) makes the invoking turn wait for the result. Skills can additionally register hooks declaratively via a `hooks:` YAML object in frontmatter, so a provenance logger or data/raw guard can be attached when a workflow skill runs rather than living permanently in settings.json.
findings.evidence: Skills docs frontmatter table, verbatim: `context` — "Set to fork to run in a forked subagent context"; `agent` — "Which subagent type to use when context: fork is set" (Explore, Plan, general-purpose, or custom subagents from .claude/agents/); `background` — "Only applies with context: fork. Set to false to wait for the forked subagent's result in the turn that invoked the skill ... Requires Claude Code v2.1.218 or later"; `hooks` — "Hooks that Claude Code registers when the skill is invoked and keeps running for the rest of the session." hooks.md gives the YAML format and the `once: true` option (honored only in skill frontmatter, ignored in settings files and agent frontmatter). Three caveats: the forked subagent does not see conversation history, so skill instructions must stand alone; isolation is of the intermediate token load (the .cif/.vcf reads), not of the returned result, which still lands in the main context; and skill-scoped hooks are session-lived after activation, not torn down when the workflow ends, unless `once: true`. Two historical bugs were plugin-scoped and are stale relative to 2.1.270 (#49559 context:fork not honored in 2.1.112; #17688 frontmatter hooks not firing in plugins, closed) — prefer project-level .claude/skills/ over plugin-packaged skills when relying on frontmatter hooks.

findings.claim: P1 — Claude Code's MCP output limits are the concrete knob for third-party bio servers that dump FASTA/mmCIF/VCF payloads: warning above 10,000 tokens, default cap 25,000, settable via `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`. Above the limit, a non-image result is spilled to a file in the session's `tool-results` directory under `~/.claude/projects/` and replaced inline by the path — a harness-level version of bio-stack's own "write to runs/, return only the path" convention. Correction to the obvious reading: raising MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS increases context consumption; it is a truncation-avoidance knob, not a token-efficiency one. For [REDACTED], consider lowering it, and for the custom nvidia-bio/nvidia-nemo servers use the per-tool `anthropic/maxResultSizeChars` annotation, which overrides the env var.
findings.evidence: /docs/en/mcp, verbatim: warning above 10,000 tokens; "the default maximum is 25,000 tokens"; `export MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS=50000`; and "when a result with no image content exceeds the limit, Claude Code saves it to a file and replaces it in the conversation with a message that names the file path ... The file goes in the session's tool-results directory under ~/.claude/projects/". Corroborated on a second official page (/docs/en/agent-sdk/mcp) with the same mechanism. Verified firsthand in session: an oversized WebFetch result was persisted to C:\Users\Manec\.claude\projects\C--Users-Manec-bio-stack\<session>\tool-results\toolu_*.txt. Limits of the mitigation: the spill only fires ABOVE the limit, so a 15k-token VCF chunk is still injected inline in full; image-bearing results (e.g. STRING network images) are excluded from the spill path; and a server declaring `anthropic/maxResultSizeChars` uses that value for text content regardless of the env var, so a third-party server can evade the spill. This replaced hard truncation in a recent release (~v2.1.92 per third-party release notes), so pin a minimum version rather than asserting it unconditionally.

findings.claim: P2 — Language servers can be wired into the agent loop declaratively rather than run ad hoc: a plugin declares them via an `lspServers` field in plugin.json or a `.lsp.json` at plugin root, with required `command` and `extensionToLanguage` plus optional `args`, `transport`, `env`, `initializationOptions`, `settings`, `workspaceFolder`, `startupTimeout`, `shutdownTimeout`, `restartOnCrash`, `maxRestarts`, `diagnostics`. Mechanically this fits `basedpyright-langserver` (already the stack's type checker), `java -jar` for the Nextflow language server, and `R --slave -e 'languageserver::run()'`. Note the naming correction: `ruff-lsp` is deprecated/archived — the current spelling is `ruff server`.
findings.evidence: plugins-reference, verbatim: "Plugins can provide Language Server Protocol (LSP) servers to give Claude real-time code intelligence while working on your codebase"; Location: ".lsp.json in plugin root, or inline in plugin.json"; required fields exactly `command` ("The LSP binary to execute (must be in PATH)") and `extensionToLanguage`; the optional-field table matches the listed set exactly. Find Tool (mapping natural language to tool specifications) and Call Tool"; "three distinct methodologies: keyword search, LLM in-context search, and embedding search" (v3 adds TF-IDF for keyword, fine-tuned GTE-Qwen2-1.5B for embeddings); and the paper's own stated bound on the LLM variant: "its application can be constrained by the finite context window of the model." Windows feasibility checked, not assumed: PyPI 1.4.1 (2026-08-12), pure-Python wheel, requires_python >=3.10, no OS classifiers; the compiled deps (faiss-cpu 1.12.0, epam.indigo, playwright, lxml) all publish cp311/py3 win_amd64 wheels, so no source build and no WSL requirement; torch-pulling packages sit behind the [ml]/[all] extras. THREE BLOCKERS TO FLAG: (1) the paper's `tooluniverse-mcp-claude` command no longer exists — the 1.4.1 wheel's console_scripts are tooluniverse, tooluniverse-mcp, tooluniverse-smcp, tooluniverse-smcp-server, tooluniverse-smcp-stdio, tooluniverse-http-api, tooluniverse-doctor, tu, tu-datastore, generate-mcp-tools; copying the paper verbatim will fail. (2) Issue #36 reports `spawn uv ENOENT` / server disconnected when GUI clients cannot see uvx on PATH. (3) Observed firsthand in this session: `plugin:tooluniverse:tooluniverse` is configured on this machine and FAILED TO CONNECT ("Skipping connection, recent failure cached") — consistent with that PATH/launcher class of problem. Do not count this gap as filled until it connects on this host. Corroborating external evidence for the retrieval-over-catalog pattern: RAG-MCP reports tool-selection accuracy 13.62% → 43.13% with prompt tokens more than halved; arXiv 2605.24660 accepts the degradation-with-catalog-size premise and reports 93.1% vs 87.1% for adaptive vs fixed-5 retrieval depth on BFCL.

findings.claim: P3 — Do NOT adopt the Augmented-Nature per-database server family as blanket coverage for UniProt/PDB/Ensembl/KEGG/STRING/Reactome/NCBI/AlphaFold/PubChem/ChEMBL. The org is real (24 repos, one per database, all built from the same TypeScript boilerplate) but near-dormant and unpublished: every repo carries the identical Dec 21, 2025 stamp from a single LICENSE sweep, the UniProt repo's last substantive code change was ~May 2025 (30 commits, 20 stars), all pin the pre-1.0 @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^0.5.0, none are on npm (no npx path — clone + tsc only), all are self-labeled "Unofficial", and README tool counts contradict their own package.json (ChEMBL README says 22 tools, package.json says 27).
findings.evidence: Org repo listing enumerates exactly 24 repos: .github plus BioOntology, ProteinAtlas, GeneOntology, Ensembl, Reactome, OpenTargets, PubChem, STRING-db, PDB, AlphaFold, KEGG, SureChEMBL, NCBI-Datasets, BioThings, ClinicalTrials, OpenGenes, OpenFDA, GTEx, BioStudies, HPO, ChEMBL, PubMed, UniProt — all showing "Updated Dec 21, 2025", with zero 2026 activity org-wide. The UniProt commit log shows that Dec 21 commit is a single "Revise LICENSE"; prior commits are a README edit (Jun 2025) and file uploads (May 2025) — i.e. ~15 months without substantive code as of 2026-09-13. Raw package.json from ChEMBL, STRING-db and UniProt are byte-level scaffold twins (same build script, same deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^0.5.0 + axios ^1.6.0, same author, MIT). registry.npmjs.org returns 404 for chembl-server / uniprot-server / string-server. Functional redundancy with what is already mounted is heavy: biocontext_kb already exposes bc_get_uniprot_protein_info, bc_get_string_interactions, bc_get_reactome_info_by_identifier, bc_query_kegg, bc_get_ensembl_id_from_gene_symbol, bc_get_alphafold_info_by_protein_symbol, plus gget-mcp (gget_pdb, gget_alphafold, gget_info, gget_seq, gget_enrichr). Note: the specific token-cost figure for the UniProt server (26 tools in 7 categories) failed verification 0-3, so the redundancy argument stands on the tool inventory above, not on that count.

findings.claim: P3 — The single-cell MCP gap remains genuinely unfilled; scmcp (github.com/scmcphub/scmcp) is not a safe answer. Its last code push was 2025-07-10 (~14 months stale), last PyPI release 0.5.0 on 2025-07-07, with 16 stars / 5 forks / 4 open issues, not archived; the entire scmcphub org's newest activity anywhere is scmcp-shared on 2025-11-29, with zero 2026 activity across all 12 repos, and Glama's directory labels it "Inactive". Its functional description (scanpy/LIANA+/decoupleR/CellRank pipeline coverage) also failed adversarial verification 1-2. Note there are two repos with this name — huang-sh/scmcp is the deprecated original that redirects to scmcphub.
findings.evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2025-07-10T16:43:17Z, stargazers_count 16, forks_count 5, open_issues_count 4, archived false, created 2025-05-09 — reproduced three ways (org listing sorted by updated shows "Updated Jul 10, 2025"; commits page shows newest commit 6542833 on that date; PyPI shows 0.5.0 on 2025-07-07 with nothing since). A WebSearch summary asserting decoupler-mcp was updated 2026-08-15 was NOT confirmed at source — GitHub's org listing places it at Jun 27, 2025; that appears to be a Glama crawl date misread. Download-volume data was unobtainable (pypistats returned HTTP 429), so "low adoption" rests on stars/forks/issues, the third-party Inactive label, no release in 14 months, and org-wide 2026 silence. Practical consequence: omics-analyst still has no maintained scanpy-facing MCP server. The stack's existing coverage of this space is the bio-research plugin skills (single-cell-rna-qc, scvi-tools) plus local scanpy/pydeseq2 — which, given the CLAUDE.md preference for scripts over tool calls and the 8 GB VRAM ceiling, is arguably the better answer than any MCP wrapper here.

input.summary: The highest-value additions to bio-stack are not new MCP servers — they are Claude Code harness mechanics the stack is not yet using, and two of them are correctness bugs rather than enhancements: the data/raw PreToolUse guard does not block unless it exits with code 2 (or emits a JSON deny), and Windows hook execution silently routes shell-form commands through Git Bash rather than PowerShell. Beyond those fixes, the largest rigor win is completing the provenance record via the ~30 documented lifecycle events the stack ignores (PostToolUseFailure makes failed runs visible in runs/provenance.jsonl, which today records only successes and therefore biases the auto-generated Methods section; SessionEnd finalizes a run; PreCompact preserves the transcript), and the largest token-efficiency win is packaging scientific-rigor protocols as skills — whose bodies load only on invocation, unlike CLAUDE.md — optionally with `context: fork` + `agent:` to drive the existing subagent roster and `hooks:` frontmatter to scope guards to a workflow. On the MCP side the ecosystem is thinner than it looks: the per-database server families that appear to blanket UniProt/PDB/Ensembl/KEGG/STRING/Reactome are near-dormant, unpublished to npm, pinned to a pre-1.0 SDK, and redundant with the already-mounted biocontext_kb and gget; the single-cell gap is real but scmcp (14 months stale, org-wide silence through 2026) does not fill it; and the one genuinely strong candidate, Harvard's ToolUniverse (2,700+ tools behind a Find Tool/Call Tool retrieval layer, pure-Python, Windows-installable), is already configured on this machine and currently failing to connect. Finally, note that MCP output above 25,000 tokens now spills to a file under ~/.claude/projects/ and returns only the path — a harness-native version of the stack's own runs/ convention, though it is a backstop above the threshold, not a substitute for it.
input.caveats:
COVERAGE GAPS — two of the five research angles produced no surviving claims and should be treated as unanswered, not as negative results: (a) Angle 2, reproducibility/provenance tooling — nothing on RO-Crate, W3C PROV/PROV-O, CWLProv, Zenodo/DOI deposition, ORCID, protocols.io, ELNs, DataLad/git-annex, or DVC survived verification, so no MCP server or CLI in that space is recommended here; (b) Angle 5, scientific-correctness guardrails — nothing on BixBench, LAB-Bench, nf-core/Snakemake/WDL conformance checking, FAIR tooling, or published evidence of where LLM agents fail in bioinformatics survived. Angle 4 is only partially covered: the LSP wiring mechanism is confirmed, but no specific language server was verified as working headlessly on Windows from Claude Code.

REFUTED MATERIAL worth knowing: the specific inventory of BioContextAI registry contents (STRING, Reactome, Ensembl, PDBe, NCBI, OLS/BioPortal, scvi-tools, anndata, cxg-census, protocols, Galaxy) was refuted 0-3 as unverified at source — query the live registry before citing any of it. The claim that registry inclusion functions as a maintenance/licensing prefilter was also refuted 0-3. scmcp's functional description was refuted 1-2.

TIME SENSITIVITY: every count and date here is a 2026-09-13 snapshot of mutable metadata. The 71-entry BioContextAI figure grows by PR; ToolUniverse's catalog went 600 → 1,000+ → 2,700+ across three paper versions in under a year; the MCP Registry's preview status could end at any time. Re-measure before quoting in a deliverable.

VERSION DEPENDENCE: local Claude Code is 2.1.270, which clears every gate cited (background:false needs 2.1.218+; MCP file-spill landed ~2.1.92; bare-prefix matcher semantics changed at 2.1.195). Anything reproduced on another machine needs a version check.

MATURITY FLAGS: LSP-via-plugin is documented but immature — an open issue reports plugins silently not recognized, Windows-specific path breakage is documented, and a third-party-reported EN... [+1099 chars]
openQuestions: Does the ToolUniverse MCP server actually connect on this Windows host? It is already configured as plugin:tooluniverse:tooluniverse and is currently failing (cached connection failure), consistent with the uvx-not-on-PATH class of bug in issue #36. Until that is resolved — and until Compact Mode is confirmed to limit the exposed surface to 4-5 discovery tools rather than injecting thousands of schemas — the single largest recommended MCP addition is unusable, and the 2,700-tool catalog is a token-budget liability rather than an asset.

What is the actual provenance/reproducibility tooling story for an LLM agent loop? No RO-Crate, PROV-O, CWLProv, Zenodo, ORCID, protocols.io, DataLad, or DVC integration survived verification. Since runs/provenance.jsonl already exists and feeds /metodos, the concrete unanswered question is whether it should be emitted in, or convertible to, a standard serialization (RO-Crate metadata or PROV-JSON) so a TCC's Methods section and its data deposition are machine-checkable — and whether any maintained MCP server or CLI does that conversion, or whether it must be written locally.

Is there any published benchmark or failure-mode study for LLM agents doing bioinformatics (BixBench, LAB-Bench, or similar) that identifies which specific steps agents get wrong — seed handling, multiple-testing correction, batch-effect handling, misreading effect sizes? This is the evidence that should determine what the rigor skills actually contain; without it, the skill content would be authored from first principles rather than from measured failure modes.

Which language server is worth wiring first given this host's state? basedpyright is already installed and is the obvious candidate, but the Nextflow language server is useless until Nextflow exists, which requires `wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04` first, and R languageserver requires an R install that is also absent. The open question is whether the LSP plugin path is stable enough on Windows to be worth the setup at all, versus continuing to run basedpyright and ruff as PostToolUse gates.

leads.why: DVC's OWN Windows guide — the single most decisive source for this question. Settles: (a) symlinks on Windows need the "Create symbolic links" user privilege, granted to Administrators by default and configured automatically ONLY by the .exe installer (not by pip/winget/choco/scoop/conda); (b) the 260-character MAX_PATH limit makes DVC fail with the misleading error "[Errno 2] No such file or directory" unless long paths are opted into via Group Policy/registry; (c) NTFS-specific performance advice (disable Search indexing, disable 8dot3 name generation above ~300K files, whitelist DVC binaries in Windows Security); (d) it recommends WSL2/Cmder/Anaconda Prompt over plain cmd.exe — relevant caveat since this machine has no Linux distro, but note DVC itself runs fine natively; (e) enforce LF line endings via .gitattributes or DVC reports spurious changes. Maintenance: DVC 3.67.1 released 2026-03-31, last commit on main 2026-08-06 — active, no 12-month flag. Action: `winget install --id Iterative.DVC` for a plain install, or download the .exe installer if you want symlink optimization.

The page that actually decides the 'few GB, must never be overwritten' question, and the one most people miss. Settles: (a) DVC's four cache link types and that the DEFAULT on Windows is **copy** — reflink is Linux-Btrfs/XFS/OCFS2 and macOS-APFS only — so a few-GB data/raw becomes ~2x on disk (raw files + .dvc/cache) unless you change cache.type; (b) hardlink and symlink modes make the workspace file READ-ONLY and require an explicit `dvc unprotect` before modification — this is the concrete, documented immutability mechanism that answers 'must never be overwritten', and it is the strongest argument for DVC over git-lfs here; (c) the NTFS hardlink cap of 1024 links per file (vs 65,000 on EXT4), a real Windows ceiling if you dedupe many identical files. Action: after `dvc init`, set `dvc config cache.type hardlink,symlink` plus `dvc config cache.protected true` to get read-only raw data without doubling disk usage — but only after granting the symlink privilege per the Windows guide above.

DataLad's own 'So… Windows… eh?' chapter — the project documenting its own Windows weaknesses, which is far more credible than third-party comparison. Settles in the project's own words: "Windows has insufficient support for symlinking and locking files (i.e., revoking write permissions)", which means the annex's read-only protection — the exact feature you want for an immutable data/raw — is the thing Windows does not give you; consequently "Datasets will have a higher disk usage on Windows machines" and "DataLad and its underlying tools are slower on Windows". Also confirms the 260-character path limit bites DataLad's hash-based key paths, that Singularity is unavailable (Docker is fine), and that cross-OS dataset interoperability is degraded. Pair with https://handbook.datalad.org/en/latest/intro/installation.html for the native no-WSL install path (`uv tool install git-annex` then `uv tool install datalad`, plus the recommended `git config --global filter.annex.process "git-annex filter-process"` for acceptable Windows performance). Maintenance: DataLad 1.6.2 released 2026-08-13, last commit 2026-09-11 — very active. Verdict this source supports: DataLad installs and runs on Windows 11 without WSL, but the handbook itself steers you to WSL2, which you do not have.

Upstream git-annex's own Windows install page (Joey Hess's site, not a mirror) — the authority on whether the Windows port is production-grade. Settles that the port is self-described as "in reasonably good shape for command-line use" but with "some known problems and parts that don't work", and that upstream tells you to run the test suite before trusting it with real data — a direct, quotable caveat for a TCC methods section. Also settles the install constraint that git-annex must live in the same folder as Git for Windows because it borrows Git's bundled libraries, and that git-annex-shell is not installed on Windows (breaking ssh remotes; workaround is copying git-annex.exe to git-annex-shell.exe). Cross-check the version/date at https://github.com/datalad/git-annex/releases — the DataLad-built Windows installer 10.20260901 is dated 2026-09-01, and upstream's changelog runs through September 2026, so this is actively maintained despite the caveats. Verdict: git-annex alone is the lowest-level and most fragile of the four on bare Windows; adopt it only via DataLad, not directly.

git-lfs's own config man page — settles the two facts that disqualify git-lfs for this project. (a) git-lfs is built around a remote LFS server; the only supported single-machine/local-disk path is the internal `lfs-standalone-file` adapter via `lfs.standalonetransferagent`, documented as "intended for use with local file:/// URLs" — workable but a niche configuration you would have to defend in a methods section. (b) A hard Windows-specific data-corruption caveat under `lfs.largefilewarning`: files 4 GiB or larger "will be corrupted when using Windows (unless smudging is disabled) with a Git for Windows version less than 2.34.0" — check `git --version` before trusting git-lfs with any multi-GB FASTQ/BAM. Crucially, git-lfs uses NO symlinks and has NO read-only protection mode: a smudged working-tree file is a normal writable file, so git-lfs gives you versioning but not the 'never overwritten' guarantee you asked for. Its advantage is that it is the only one of the four with zero Windows filesystem caveats around symlinks or MAX_PATH.

Primary release record for git-lfs — settles current version and maintenance date, and the Windows packaging question. Latest is v3.8.0 published 2026-08-28 (built with Go 1.27; adds zstd-compressed object download), well inside the 12-month freshness window. Confirms the project ships a signed Windows installer containing both x86 and x64 binaries, so installation on Windows 11 is a non-issue — `winget install GitHub.GitLFS` — and note Git for Windows already bundles a git-lfs that the standalone installer will not upgrade (see issue #2587), a real version-skew trap given the 4 GiB corruption caveat above. Use this page to pin an exact version in your Methods section rather than citing 'latest'.
