input.summary: The question splits along two orthogonal axes: the two target traits (teeth and tail), each with its own gene-loss and developmental-program literature, and the evidence layers around them (comparative outgroup genomics, prior wet-lab atavism experiments, and in silico design tooling). I gave one angle per trait, one to the crocodilian/archosaur outgroup that defines the intact ancestral toolkit, one to the experimental precedents deliberately merged with the replication and "dino-chicken" critiques so skeptical and ethical framing surfaces alongside the claims it targets, and one to the computational and germline-editing feasibility stack.

results.title: Genome modelling and design across all domains of life with Evo 2 (Nature)
results.snippet: Primary source for the one model that could plausibly score the edits in this project: 7B/40B StripedHyena-2 trained on 8.85 Tb across 15,032 eukaryotic genomes (so archosaur genomes are in-distribution), 1 Mb context that can span distal enhancers, and zero-shot coding + non-coding variant effect scoring via delta log-likelihood. Also the paper's own caveats matter for the angle: benchmarking is overwhelmingly human/ClinVar-anchored (plus BRCA1 and prokaryotic essentiality), so transferring the pathogenicity calibration to chicken pseudogene lesions (ENAM/AMBN frameshifts) or to avian CNEE scoring is an extrapolation the paper does not validate. This is also the model exposed through the project's mcp__nvidia-bio__evo2_score / evo2_likelihood NIM endpoints.

results.title: DART-Eval: A Comprehensive DNA Language Model Evaluation Benchmark on Regulatory DNA
results.snippet: The load-bearing counterweight to Evo 2 optimism. DART-Eval evaluates DNA LMs (including Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA, Mistral-DNA) on graded regulatory tasks — discriminating cCREs from background, TF motif/footprint recovery, cell-type-specific activity, and quantitative variant-effect on MPRA/caQTL data — and reports that zero-shot likelihoods and even fine-tuned genomic LMs frequently fail to beat far cheaper supervised CNN baselines (ChromBPNet-class) on the tasks that actually matter for enhancer engineering. Directly bounds what can be claimed when scoring a designed cis-regulatory edit in a non-human vertebrate; pair with the companion benchmarking literature (e.g. Benchmarking DNA foundation models, PMC12663285) before asserting any model-derived enhancer call.

results.title: An atlas of regulatory elements in chicken: a resource for chicken genetics and genomics (Science Advances)
results.snippet: The ENCODE-analogue resource the design step requires: full FAANG core-assay annotation of Gallus gallus — 217 new datasets (140 ChIP-seq for H3K4me3/H3K4me1/H3K27ac/H3K27me3 + input, 28 ATAC-seq, 27 RNA-seq across 14 tissues, 18 RRBS), plus uniform reanalysis of 160 existing chicken datasets — yielding promoter/enhancer/insulator calls and activity states. This is the empirical substrate for asking whether the odontogenic regulatory loci that remain intact in birds (BMP4, SHH, PITX2, MSX1/2, BARX1, LEF1, EDA/EDAR) still carry accessible cis-regulatory elements in mandibular/craniofacial tissue, and for anchoring any model-predicted enhancer edit to measured chromatin rather than to a language-model score alone. Note the atlas is adult/whole-tissue biased; HH-staged craniofacial ATAC is sparser and must be sourced separately.

results.title: Genome Editing in the Chicken: From PGC-Mediated Germline Transmission to Advanced Applications
results.snippet: Answers the feasibility half of the angle directly: chicken is the only vertebrate whose primordial germ cells can be stably expanded in vitro, transfected, clonally selected for a precise edit, and then reintroduced into surrogate host embryos for germline transmission — so a multi-locus atavism construct is technically routable in Aves in a way it is not in any other non-mammalian amniote. Recent review covering PGC culture conditions, CRISPR/Cas9 HDR and NHEJ knockouts, transposon vectors, sterile surrogate hosts (iCaspase9/DDX4 ablation) and realistic germline transmission rates. Complements the earlier foundational work (Dimitrov et al. 2016, PLOS ONE, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0154303, CRISPR-mediated HR in PGCs) and the 2025 Frontiers in Genome Editing review of concepts, applications and regulatory issues.

results.title: DNA damage hypersensitivity in chicken primordial germ cells limits CRISPR-Cas9 editing and supports an shRNA-based screening approach (preprint)
results.snippet: The caveat that constrains any multi-edit atavism plan: chicken PGCs are reported to be hypersensitive to double-strand-break-induced apoptosis, which caps achievable Cas9 editing efficiency and makes stacking many independent nuclease cuts (e.g. repairing seven pseudogenized enamel-matrix loci plus axial-elongation edits in one lineage) far harder than single-locus proofs of concept suggest. Practical implication: favour base and prime editing (no DSB) over nuclease multiplexing. FLAG: bioRxiv preprint, not peer-reviewed and to my knowledge not independently replicated — treat the magnitude of the effect as provisional and cite it as a hypothesis about editing ceilings, not an established parameter.

results.title: Intrinsically disordered proteins drive enamel formation via an evolutionarily conserved self-assembly motif (PNAS)
results.snippet: Sets the hard limit on the structural-modelling arm of the project. Amelogenin and ameloblastin are intrinsically disordered proteins — globally unfolded in solution with transient PPII/extended-beta segments — whose biological function is supramolecular ribbon self-assembly driven by a Y/F-x-x-Y/L/F-x-Y/F motif conserved from the first tetrapods to humans, not a folded tertiary structure. Consequence for methodology: single-chain folding predictors (AlphaFold/ESMFold/Boltz, and the project's hosted fold_protein NIM) will return uninformative low-pLDDT models for AMELX/AMBN/ENAM, and a resurrected avian enamel protein cannot be scored by pLDDT; the meaningful in silico readouts are disorder/IDR prediction, motif conservation, and coarse-grained or MD assembly simulation. Companion primary work: Wald et al., ameloblastin exon-5 N-terminal ribbon assembly (J Biol Chem).

results.title: Xia et al. 2024, Nature — On the genetic basis of tail-loss evolution in humans and apes (TBXT AluY)
results.snippet: The primary paper for the hominoid tail-loss mechanism named in the research question. A hominoid-specific AluY inserted in TBXT intron 6 pairs with a simian AluSx1 in the antisense orientation, forming a stem-loop in the pre-mRNA that traps exon 6 and produces an exon-skipped TBXT isoform. Validated two ways: CRISPR-Cas9 deletion of the AluY in human ESCs restores normal splicing, and mice engineered to express the exon-skipped isoform show absent/shortened tails. Note for the parent synthesis: the phenotype is heterozygote-dependent and incompletely penetrant, and the paper also reports a neural-tube-defect cost — so it is a gain-of-isoform, not a simple loss-of-function, and is the single best worked example of a discrete, dateable, transposon-driven cis-lesion that shortens a tail. DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-07095-8.

results.title: Aires et al. 2019, Developmental Cell — Tail Bud Progenitor Activity Relies on a Network Comprising Gdf11, Lin28, and Hox13 Genes
results.snippet: The single most load-bearing mechanistic paper for the 'how do you make a tail longer' half of the question: it wires GDF11 → HOX13 → LIN28 (→ let-7) into one epistatic cassette controlling axial-progenitor proliferative capacity after the trunk-to-tail transition. Hoxb13 and Hoxc13 are the most strongly downregulated genes in Gdf11-/- tail buds; Lin28 loss shortens the tail and sustained Lin28 expression in axial progenitors adds caudal vertebrae. This is the node an in silico design would target, and it supplies directionality (which way each perturbation pushes vertebra count) that the pygostyle literature alone does not. DOI 10.1016/j.devcel.2018.12.004.

results.title: Rashid et al. 2014, EvoDevo — From dinosaurs to birds: a tail of evolution
results.snippet: The review explicitly named in the research question, and the one source that connects the mouse/chick axial-termination genetics to the avian fossil record. Surveys 23 mouse mutations producing short, fused tails, notes that at least half sit in the Notch/Wnt somite-boundary pathway, and argues that caudal-somite reduction and pygostyle patterning are both set early, during somitogenesis at the tail-bud stage — i.e. the avian tail was truncated by changes in axial extension, not by a distal amputation program. Also frames the Archaeopteryx/Caudipteryx caudal-count comparison. Caveat to flag: the gene-to-phenotype mapping here is largely argument-by-analogy from mouse mutants, not from avian functional genetics. DOI 10.1186/2041-9139-5-25.

results.title: Denans, Iimura & Pourquié 2015, eLife — Hox genes control vertebrate body elongation by collinear Wnt repression
results.snippet: Directly avian: worked in the chicken embryo tail bud, so it is the closest thing to a mechanism established in Gallus rather than transferred from mouse. Progressively more posterior Hox paralogs (9-13) repress Wnt activity with increasing strength, producing graded repression of Brachyury/TBXT, reduced mesoderm ingression from the progenitor zone, and a slowdown of elongation. This supplies the causal chain HOX13 → Wnt → TBXT that links the two halves of the target trait, and identifies posterior-Hox timing (heterochrony) rather than gene presence/absence as the lever — important because birds retain intact HOX13 paralogs. DOI 10.7554/eLife.04379.

results.title: Rashid et al. 2018, Scientific Reports — Avian tail ontogeny, pygostyle formation, and interpretation of juvenile Mesozoic specimens
results.snippet: Establishes the ontogenetic timing that constrains any 'long bony tail' experiment: in extant birds the distal caudals do not fuse into a pygostyle until near skeletal maturity, and vertebral-process mineralization likewise occurs long after hatching, with the same post-hatching fusion inferred in a juvenile enantiornithine and a subadult basal ornithuromorph. Consequence for in silico design: the free-caudal count (the embryonic, somitogenesis-set variable) and the fusion event (a late post-hatching process) are separable targets, so an embryonic axial-elongation edit and a fusion-suppression edit are different interventions on different timelines. DOI 10.1038/s41598-018-27336-x.

results.title: Amândio et al. 2024, PNAS — CTCF-dependent insulation of Hoxb13 and the heterochronic control of tail length
results.snippet: Most directly useful result for the question's in silico cis-regulatory-editing angle: tail length is tuned not by coding changes to HOXB13 but by CTCF-boundary insulation controlling when Hoxb13 is activated relative to the rest of the cluster — removing the insulation shifts activation timing and shortens the tail. This makes TAD-boundary/CTCF-site architecture around the HoxB cluster a concrete, scoreable target class for genomic language models (Evo 2 / Nucleotide Transformer) and for chicken ATAC-seq enhancer atlases, rather than the gene bodies themselves. Recent and, as of this search, apparently not independently replicated outside the originating group — treat the specific boundary element as single-study. DOI 10.1073/pnas.2414865121.

results.title: Harris et al. 2006, "The Development of Archosaurian First-Generation Teeth in a Chicken Mutant", Current Biology 16(4):371-377 (doi:10.1016/j.cub.2005.12.047)
results.snippet: The single strongest experimental atavism precedent for teeth without cross-species tissue grafting. The talpid2 (later mapped to C2CD3) mutant shifts the oral/non-oral ectoderm boundary so the lateral signaling center again overlies competent odontogenic mesenchyme; BMP4 and SHH expression are restored in the mandibular dental lamina and conical, caniniform outgrowths form that resemble crocodilian first-generation rudimentary teeth. Critically for the question's 'what was actually recovered' framing: these are tooth germs with a saccate/conical morphology, NOT mineralized enamel — talpid2 embryos are lethal before any enamel matrix stage, and the enamel matrix gene set is pseudogenized anyway. The paper also reports transient induction in wild-type chick via viral misexpression. Single-lab result on a rare lethal mutant; the phenotype has been reproduced in the talpid2 line but no independent line has recapitulated it.

results.title: Sire, Delgado & Girondot 2008, "Hen's teeth with enamel cap: from dream to impossibility", BMC Evolutionary Biology 8:246 (doi:10.1186/1471-2148-8-246)
results.snippet: The key skeptical counterweight — it explicitly asks whether the tooth-germ atavism literature could ever yield an enamel-capped hen's tooth and answers no. Surveys AMEL, AMBN, ENAM and DSPP in the Gallus gallus genome, documenting the specific lesions (frameshifts, stop codons, outright loss), dates the inactivation to the bird stem ~100-80 Ma, and directly addresses the Kollar & Fisher 1980 problem: possible contamination of mouse molar mesenchyme by residual mouse epithelium makes the 'chick ameloblasts deposited enamel' interpretation uncertain. This is the paper that separates 'rudimentary conical tooth germ' (achievable, demonstrated) from 'mineralized enamel' (requires resurrecting dead genes, not derepressing latent ones). Companion evidence: Al-Hashimi et al. 2010 MBE on the chicken ENAM pseudogene (https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/27/9/2078/1009898).

results.title: Chen et al. 2000, "Conservation of early odontogenic signaling pathways in Aves", PNAS 97(18):10044-10049 (doi:10.1073/pnas.160245097)
results.snippet: Defines exactly which odontogenic regulatory genes remain intact and expressed in chick versus which are missing — the gene-by-gene inventory the in-silico edit design needs. FGF8, PITX2, BARX1 and PAX9 still mark a potential chick odontogenic region, while BMP4, MSX1 and MSX2 are absent from the presumptive chick dental lamina; exogenous BMP4 restores Msx expression and the chick lamina responds. Supports the 'loss of odontogenic BMP4 expression arrests tooth development' model, i.e. the block is cis-regulatory/positional rather than a loss of the mesenchymal toolkit. Note the framing tension with Mitsiadis 2003, which locates the deficit in avian neural-crest mesenchyme rather than in epithelial signaling — the two are not fully reconciled in the literature.

results.title: Mitsiadis, Chéraud, Sharpe & Fontaine-Pérus 2003, "Development of teeth in chick embryos after mouse neural crest transplantations", PNAS 100(11):6541-6545 (doi:10.1073/pnas.1137104100)
results.snippet: The chimera experiment that reframed Kollar & Fisher: mouse neural tube grafted into chick host so mouse neural-crest-derived ectomesenchyme meets *chick* oral epithelium in situ. Tooth germs form, showing avian oral epithelium retains the inductive signaling competence and that the odontogenic deficit sits on the crest/mesenchyme side. Unlike the 1980 intraocular graft it is far harder to explain by residual mouse epithelial contamination, since donor and host tissues are distinguishable by quail/mouse markers — but it still yields early tooth germs, not enamel. Follow-up review framing the limits: Mitsiadis et al. 2006 J Exp Zool B, 'Waking-up the sleeping beauty: recovery of the ancestral bird odontogenic program' (doi:10.1002/jez.b.21094).

results.title: Bhullar et al. 2015, "A molecular mechanism for the origin of a key evolutionary innovation, the bird beak and palate…", Evolution 69(7):1665-1677 (doi:10.1111/evo.12684)
results.snippet: The best-documented non-dental avian atavism experiment and the source of the 'dino-chicken' media cycle the question asks about. Inhibiting the frontonasal ectodermal zone (SHH/FGF8) and midfacial WNT-responsive signaling in chick embryos produced premaxillae that cluster geometrically with ancestral archosaur fossils rather than with beaked birds, with a correlated palatine reversion. Important caveats for the replication/spectacle angle: embryos were not hatched, the phenotype is a quantitative shape shift scored by geometric morphometrics rather than a discrete 'snout', and Bhullar himself framed it against spectacle — 'our goal here was to understand the molecular underpinnings of an important evolutionary transition, not to create a dino-chicken simply for the sake of it.' Independent replication of the double-inhibition phenotype is thin.

results.title: Kollar & Fisher 1980, "Tooth Induction in Chick Epithelium: Expression of Quiescent Genes for Enamel Synthesis", Science 207(4434):993-995 (doi:10.1126/science.7352302)
results.snippet: The origin of the claim that chick epithelium can be pushed all the way to ameloblast differentiation and enamel matrix deposition — and the canonical example in this field of a single, non-replicated study that later evidence undercuts. Intraocular grafts of E5 chick oral epithelium plus E16-18 mouse molar mesenchyme reportedly produced crowns with differentiated ameloblasts. Flag it as contested rather than citing it as evidence for enamel: the residual-mouse-epithelium contamination objection (Sire et al. 2008; Mitsiadis et al. 2003) has never been resolved, no one has reproduced enamel-depositing chick ameloblasts in 45 years, and the chicken enamel matrix genes are pseudogenes, so the result as stated has no molecular substrate. Compare the earlier lizard-quail recombination work (Kollar & Fisher's precedent, J Morphol 176:307).

results.title: Green et al. 2014, Science — Three crocodilian genomes reveal ancestral patterns of evolution among archosaurs
results.snippet: The anchor outgroup resource for the whole project: draft genomes of Alligator mississippiensis, Crocodylus porosus and Gavialis gangeticus (DOI 10.1126/science.1254449; PMID 25504731), published as the companion to the Avian Phylogenomics/Meredith tooth-gene papers in the same Science package. Establishes that crocodilians evolve exceptionally slowly at every level (substitutions, indels, TE content/movement, gene-family turnover, chromosomal synteny), so the *rapid* evolution — including the genome shrinkage and gene/CNEE loss that accompanies avian edentulism and the pygostyle — is derived in the bird stem, not ancestral to archosaurs. That polarity is what licenses using Alligator as the intact-toolkit reference against which Gallus lesions in ENAM/AMBN/AMELX/DSPP/MMP20/AMTN/ODAM are scored as losses rather than divergence. Also reconstructs a partial archosaur common-ancestor genome, which is the natural template if edits are to be framed as reversions rather than de novo design. Free PDF of the intro at https://pgl.soe.ucsc.edu/green14.pdf.

results.title: Wu et al. 2013, PNAS — Specialized stem cell niche enables repetitive renewal of alligator teeth
results.snippet: Primary mechanistic account of crocodilian polyphyodonty and the single best-characterised intact amniote dental lamina. Each of the ~80 alligator teeth is a 'tooth family unit' (functional tooth + successional tooth + dental lamina), replaceable up to ~50 times; multiple mitotic labelling maps quiescent odontogenic progenitors to the distal enlarged bulge of the dental lamina, activated on natural exfoliation or experimental extraction, with cycle initiation tied to β-catenin/Wnt activity in that bulge. This is the tissue-level structure that birds lack entirely: any in silico plan to restore mineralised teeth has to specify whether it targets first-generation tooth germs only (the talpid2/Harris outcome) or the successional lamina niche, and this paper defines what the latter would require. Supplies the Wnt/β-catenin entry point that connects directly to the Bhullar and Chen-type epithelial manipulations in chick.

results.title: Tsai et al. 2016, J Dent Res 95(13):1501–1510 — The Molecular Circuit Regulating Tooth Development in Crocodilians
results.snippet: Follow-on to Wu 2013 from the same USC group (PMCID PMC5119682): transcriptomic/expression profiling of the alligator dental lamina that names the actual signalling circuit — the BMP/SHH/WNT/FGF and associated transcription-factor set — operating in an archosaur that still makes enamel-capped teeth. This is the direct comparator for the question of which odontogenic regulators (BMP4, SHH, PITX2, MSX1/2, BARX1, RUNX2, FGF8, LEF1, EDA/EDAR) remain intact and inducible in Gallus: the crocodilian circuit tells you which nodes the bird retains versus which upstream inputs are genuinely missing. Practically, it is the gene list a comparative RNA-seq or enhancer-scoring exercise (Evo 2 / DNABERT-2 style) should be benchmarked against, because it is measured in the outgroup rather than inferred from mouse.

results.title: Sackton et al. 2019, Science — Convergent regulatory evolution and loss of flight in paleognathous birds
results.snippet: The methodological template for the CNEE side of the question: builds a large avian conserved non-exonic element set on a whole-genome alignment and shows that repeated loss of a complex trait (flight) maps to convergent acceleration in non-coding regulatory elements near developmental genes, with little signal in protein-coding sequence. Directly transferable to asking which CNEEs were lost or accelerated on the avian stem around the odontogenic and caudal-axis loci — and it argues that the edits required for atavism are more likely cis-regulatory than coding, which reframes the 'restore the enamel gene set' plan. Open copy at https://dash.harvard.edu/bitstream/1/39865637/1/Sackton_et_al_DASH_version.pdf; the Edwards-lab CNEE marker framework is set out in Syst Biol 66(6):1028 (https://academic.oup.com/sysbio/article/66/6/1028/3868964). Note the 2019 flight-loss conclusions have been debated on alignment/statistical grounds.

results.title: Feng et al. 2020, Nature — Dense sampling of bird diversity increases power of comparative genomics (B10K phase II)
results.snippet: 363 genomes covering 92.4% of bird families, 267 newly sequenced for B10K phase II; the resource that makes lineage-specific loss claims testable across Aves rather than in a handful of model species. Relevant two ways: it is the denominator for checking whether the ENAM/AMBN/AMELX/DSPP/MMP20 frameshifts and stop codons Meredith et al. reported really are shared-derived across all crown birds (the single-loss hypothesis) or whether dense sampling reveals independent/staggered lesions, and it provides the alignment depth needed to call CNEE presence/absence on the avian stem with Alligator as outgroup. Data portal: https://b10k.genomics.cn/ . Caveat for the user's project: many B10K assemblies are short-read and fragmented, so absence of a short non-coding element in a given assembly is weak evidence of real loss.

results.title: Bornelöv et al. 2017, Mol Biol Evol 34(12):3123 — Avian Genomes Revisited: Hidden Genes Uncovered and the Rates versus Traits Paradox in Birds
results.snippet: The necessary skeptical control on every 'birds lost gene X' claim, including the tooth gene set. Lovell et al. (2014) inferred ~274 genes lost in the bird lineage from syntenic blocks; this paper shows a large fraction of apparent avian gene absences are assembly and annotation artefacts — GC-rich, repeat-dense, microchromosome/dot-chromosome regions that short-read assemblies systematically drop — and recovers many as 'hidden' rather than lost. For an in silico atavism design this is decisive: before proposing to restore a pseudogenised locus one must confirm the lesion is real in a long-read assembly rather than a gap, and the same caution applies to missing CNEEs. results.title: Meredith, Zhang, Gilbert, Jarvis & Springer (2014) — Evidence for a single loss of mineralized teeth in the common avian ancestor. Science 346(6215):1254390
results.snippet: The keystone primary paper the whole question rests on. Screened 48 bird genomes from the Avian Phylogenomics Project across the dentin gene DSPP and enamel genes ENAM, AMELX, AMTN, MMP20, recovering inactivating mutations (frameshifts, stop codons, splice-site and exon losses) SHARED by all 48 taxa — the argument for a single edentulism event in the crown-bird ancestor rather than convergent losses. Uses the frameshift-accumulation / dN:dS relaxed-selection clock to date enamel-cap loss to ~116 Ma, and frames the 'two-step' model in which tooth loss and keratinous beak development co-evolved. DOI: 10.1126/science.1254390; PubMed 25504730. Caveats worth flagging for the parent question: the inference rests on the 2014 short-read B10K/Avian Phylogenomics assemblies, and the 116 Ma date is a single-study molecular estimate whose confidence interval depends on the assumed neutral indel rate.

results.title: Sire, Delgado & Girondot (2008) — Hen's teeth with enamel cap: from dream to impossibility. BMC Evolutionary Biology 8:246
results.snippet: The single most important counterweight to the 'dino-chicken' framing and directly answers part (2) of the question: it audits the chicken genome for the enamel matrix protein toolkit and concludes that AMELX survives only as an invalidated (pseudogenized) full-length copy, while AMBN and ENAM were outright DELETED following chromosomal rearrangement in the avian stem lineage — not merely mutated. The practical consequence is that no epithelial-mesenchymal recombination or signalling manipulation can recover a mineralized enamel cap in Gallus, because the structural genes are physically absent; at most one recovers rudimentary, first-generation conical tooth germs (as in talpid2). Essential for separating 'odontogenic potential retained' from 'enamel producible'. DOI: 10.1186/1471-2148-8-246.

results.title: Al-Hashimi, Lafont, Delgado, Kawasaki & Sire (2010) — The enamelin genes in lizard, crocodile, and frog and the pseudogene in the chicken provide new insights on enamelin evolution in tetrapods. Molecular Biology and Evolution 27(9):2078-2094
results.snippet: Provides the lesion-level detail the question asks for: characterizes the ENAM pseudogene remnant in Gallus gallus exon by exon and contrasts it against INTACT, functional ENAM in Crocodylus/Alligator, Anolis and Xenopus — i.e. it simultaneously documents the chicken lesion and establishes the crocodilian intact-toolkit outgroup needed for part (4). This predates Meredith 2014 and was based on targeted sequencing rather than short-read WGS assembly, so it independently corroborates the chicken ENAM lesions against the assembly-artifact objection. DOI: 10.1093/molbev/msq098; PubMed 20403965.

results.title: Meredith, Gatesy & Springer (2013) — Molecular decay of enamel matrix protein genes in turtles and other edentulous amniotes. BMC Evolutionary Biology 13:20
results.snippet: The methodological precursor to Meredith 2014 and the broader amniote framework: shows AMBN, AMELX, ENAM, AMTN, MMP20 and DSPP carry inactivating mutations across every independently edentulous amniote clade examined (turtles, birds, pangolins, anteaters, baleen whales). Critically for the bird case, it reports inactivated AMBN, AMEL and ENAM copies in Galloanserae, Passeriformes and Psittaciformes with SHARED frameshifts that predate the basal neognath split — the pre-2014 evidence for deep, pre-Neognathae timing of the lesions. Also argues enamel formation is the only unique amniote function of these genes, which matters for predicting pleiotropic consequences of restoring them in silico. DOI: 10.1186/1471-2148-13-20; PubMed 23342979.

results.title: Emerling et al. — Genomic data suggest parallel dental vestigialization within the xenarthran radiation (bioRxiv 2022.12.09.519446; PCI Genomics recommended)
results.snippet: The best available methodological challenge to the single-loss inference style used by Meredith 2014. Same 11-core-dental-gene / shared-inactivating-mutation / dN:dS relaxed-selection toolkit, but applied to Xenarthra it recovers PARALLEL, stepwise vestigialization rather than one ancestral event — with dento-gingival-junction genes (AMTN, ODAM, ACPT) inactivating on a different schedule from the amelogenesis genes. Shows that shared pseudogenization can be assembled from partially independent losses and that 'single loss' conclusions are sensitive to taxon sampling and to which gene subset anchors the date. Use it to argue the avian 116 Ma figure should be treated as a loss window with per-gene heterogeneity, not a single event date. Peer-reviewed via Peer Community In Genomics.

results.title: Gasse, Silvent & Sire (2015) — Amelotin: an enamel matrix protein that experienced distinct evolutionary histories in amphibians, sauropsids and mammals. BMC Evolutionary Biology 15:47
results.snippet: Fills the AMTN/ODAM (secretory calcium-binding phosphoprotein, dento-gingival junction) half of the gene set that the enamelin/amelogenin literature under-covers, and is the sauropsid-specific treatment: traces AMTN across squamates, crocodilians and birds, showing lineage-distinct histories and pseudogenization in the avian lineage. Relevant because AMTN and ODAM function at the junctional epithelium rather than in the enamel matrix proper, so their decay timing is an independent clock from ENAM/AMELX and is exactly the kind of per-gene heterogeneity that complicates a single-loss reading. DOI: 10.1186/s12862-015-0329-x.

claims.claim: In Gallus gallus the pygostyle is NOT formed embryonically: the four core pygostyle vertebrae are still separate 8 days post-hatch, fuse progressively in a distal-to-proximal direction, and are fully fused only by ~5 months of age — i.e. the pygostyle is a post-hatching ossified-bone ankylosis event, not an embryonic cartilage-patterning event. This directly constrains where an in silico edit aimed at restoring a long bony tail would have to act (segmentation/somite number in the embryo vs. post-natal fusion), and the paper explicitly corrects earlier alcian-blue wholemount studies that reported embryonic fusion.
claims.quote: In the chicken, pygostyle fusion is progressive, and occurs in the distal to proximal direction. At eight days post-hatching, all four core pygostyle vertebrae are separate and distinct. By five months of age, the core pygostyle vertebrae are fully fused. Pygostyle formation in the chicken, therefore, occurs as a post-hatch event between ossified vertebrae.

claims.claim: Post-hatching pygostyle formation is a conserved trait across modern birds, not a chicken-specific artifact of domestication: microCT of 15 juvenile specimens spanning 13 taxa (plus a 14th from skeletal specimens), covering all three major clades (Neoaves, Galloanserae, Palaeognathae), showed unfused or partially fused pygostyles in every juvenile except two or three near adult size. Timing is loosely coupled to skeletal maturity rather than absolute age (chicken ~5 months; 5.5-month emu still largely unfused; ~3-week California scrub-jay fully fused).
claims.quote: The three major avian groups, neoaves, galloanseriforms, and paleognaths, were represented in these scans, indicating that post-hatching pygostyle formation is a conserved feature in modern birds, and the same appears to be the case in Mesozoic birds.

claims.claim: The number of caudal vertebrae incorporated into the pygostyle is not fixed across Aves: Early Cretaceous confuciusornithids and enantiornithines had larger pygostyles relative to femur length (body-size proxy) than any other extinct or extant bird measured, with microCT of the subadult Confuciusornis pygostyle NGMC 98-8-2 indicating ~8 ankylosed vertebrae (counted from unfused neural arch components), versus a maximum of 5 among the extant birds surveyed (Humboldt penguin). Measurements: 152 adult extant specimens / 64 species plus 40 extinct specimens from published sources.
claims.quote: MicroCT scanning of a pygostyle (NGMC 98-8-2;) indicates that in this subadult, approximately eight vertebrae ankylosed into the pygostyle, evident by the number of unfused neural arch components... In the extant birds analyzed in this study, the greatest number of pygostyle vertebrae was five, estimated for the Humboldt penguin

claims.claim: The authors restate (from prior mouse-mutation analyses, not from new data generated here) that mutations causing caudal vertebral fusion usually also reduce caudal vertebral number, and carry pleiotropic effects producing additional axial and limb bone fusions — the basis for the hypothesis that the abrupt long-to-short-tail transition required relatively few Cretaceous mutations. This is the paper's only genetic-mechanism content; it names no specific genes (no GDF11, TBXT, HOX13, WNT3A, LIN28A), reports no apoptosis/programmed-cell-death data for the avian tail bud, and is inherited from the earlier Rashid et al. review rather than tested here.
claims.quote: These analyses were conducted in mice, and indicated that mutations that cause tail vertebrae to fuse also usually decrease the number of caudal vertebrae. Additional pleiotropic effects of tail shortening and tail fusing mutations include more extensive vertebral fusion along the axial column, as well as peripheral fusions in the limbs, akin to the bone fusions observed in Pygostylia birds.

claims.claim: Intervertebral discs do form between prospective pygostyle vertebrae in the chicken and are then eliminated by tissue remodeling, with complete trabecular remodeling by 1.5 years erasing all trace of the original separate vertebrae; the authors interpret the transient discs as a retained atavistic trait of the long-tailed ancestor. The spinal cord also persists inside the fused pygostyle and was likewise observed in a Confuciusornis pygostyle. This identifies a transient developmental window in which ancestral long-tail architecture is still present and, in principle, interruptible.
claims.quote: Intervertebral discs, for example, initially form but are subsequently lost by tissue remodeling, though the discs within the pygostyle are narrower than in the free caudal vertebrae... The pygostyle discs may be an atavistic trait, indicative of a long-tailed ancestor.

claims.claim: The avian beak is structurally defined by fused premaxillae that are geometrically distinct from the premaxillae of ancestral archosaurs, a difference the authors establish quantitatively from combined fossil and extant comparative data rather than by qualitative description.

claims.claim: The two avian facial signaling centers are hierarchically coupled: experimentally altering the earlier frontonasal ectodermal zone (FEZ) was sufficient to shift the later midfacial WNT-responsive domain back to the ancestral amniote pattern — implying an upstream single-node intervention can cascade to reset a downstream regulatory domain, which is the kind of leverage point an in silico edit-design pipeline would target.
claims.quote: Altering the FEZ altered later WNT responsiveness to the ancestral pattern.

claims.claim: The induced reversion was not restricted to the premaxilla: the palatal region of the treated chicken embryos was also shifted toward a more ancestral (non-avian archosaur) phenotype, consistent with the functional integration of premaxilla and palate in the kinetic avian beak — so the beak-to-snout manipulation transforms a coupled skeletal module, not a single bone.
claims.quote: The palatal region was also altered to a more ancestral phenotype. This is consistent with the fossil record and with the tight functional association of avian premaxillae and palate in forming a kinetic beak.

claims.claim: Hominoid tail loss is attributed to a hominoid-specific AluY insertion in intron 6 of TBXT (Brachyury) that base-pairs with an ancestral, reverse-orientation AluSx1 element in intron 5, forming an exon-flanking inverted repeat that traps exon 6 in a stem-loop and produces an in-frame exon-6-skipped TBXT isoform. CRISPR deletion of either Alu element in human ES cells abolishes the isoform, establishing that both elements are required. Mechanism is intronic/cis-regulatory-splicing, not coding-sequence change: the authors explicitly failed to find causal coding variants across 140 tail-development genes (85,064 hominoid-specific SNVs, 5,533 deletions, 13,820 insertions screened).
claims.quote: We demonstrate that this Alu element-inserted into an intron of the TBXT gene-pairs with a neighbouring ancestral Alu element encoded in the reverse genomic orientation and leads to a hominoid-specific alternative splicing event.

claims.claim: Tail length in mouse is a quantitative function of the RATIO of exon-skipped to full-length Tbxt transcript in the E10.5 tail bud, not a binary on/off switch. Heterozygous exon-6-deletion mice showed incomplete penetrance (21/63 heterozygotes with tail phenotypes vs 0/35 wild-type littermates); a mouse line with an inverted 220 bp reverse-complement pair flanking exon 6 (low isoform abundance) had only ~10% shorter tails; compound heterozygotes with higher exon-skipped abundance showed 19/19 complete absence of external tail. This makes isoform dosage the tunable lever for axial-elongation phenotypes.
claims.quote: Specifically, 21 out of the 63 heterozygous mice showed tail phenotypes, whereas none of their 35 wild-type littermates showed phenotypes

claims.claim: The authors state explicitly that reverting the AluY lesion in modern hominoids would NOT be expected to restore a tail, because additional (unidentified) genetic changes likely stabilized the no-tail phenotype after or before the insertion. This is a directly transferable caution for any in silico atavism design: reversing the single best-documented causal lesion is insufficient to reverse a long-fixed morphological loss, and the same logic applies to reversing avian pygostyle/edentulism lesions.
claims.quote: Such a possible set of genetic events suggest that a change to the AluY element in modern hominoids would be unlikely to result in the reappearance of the tail.

claims.claim: Exon skipping by this mechanism is sequence-agnostic: inserting a 297 bp reverse-complement of an endogenous mouse Tbxt intron-5 sequence (non-Alu) into intron 6 produced the same exon-skipping event, and did so more efficiently than the human AluY/AluSx1 pair (297/297 vs 228/297 stem identity). Any inverted repeat pair flanking an exon can drive skipping, which makes this a general, designable cis-element architecture for engineering isoform ratios in non-human vertebrates.
claims.quote: our results demonstrated that a completely different (non-Alu) inverted repeat sequence in the introns flanking an exon may also lead to exon skipping

claims.claim: Perturbing the TBXT isoform balance carries severe pleiotropic cost: homozygous exon-6-deletion mice were never recovered viable — embryos either arrested around E9 or developed spinal cord malformations lethal at birth — and pups exhibited neural-tube-closure defects resembling spina bifida. The authors frame tail loss as carrying an adaptive trade-off of neural tube defects (~1 in 1,000 human neonates). claims.quote: The insertion of the CTCF cassette fully suppresses the Hoxb13 gain of function, even with a much shorter distance between Hoxb9 and Hoxb13. claims.claim: Two occupied CTCF sites (CBS7 and CBS8) account for most of the insulation, and their orientation is not critical — inverting the full cassette, or leaving only two sites in either orientation, produced comparable insulation. claims.quote: Therefore, loop extrusion initiated from this part of the "spacer" DNA would be blocked or delayed mostly by CBS7 and CBS8. claims.claim: A survey of 157 informative genome sequences shows the Hoxb9–Hoxb13 spacer length is broadly maintained across vertebrates while its DNA sequence is poorly conserved (even between mouse inbred strains); the shortest amniote spacers are ~6× the engineered 6.6 kb in Aves (i.e. ~40 kb) and ≥8× in placental mammals. ---
name: evo-devo
description: Genômica comparativa evolutiva e evo-devo — perda gênica e pseudogenização, reconstrução de estado ancestral, polarização por grupo externo, elementos não-codificantes conservados, heterocronia, e desenho in silico de reversão de caráter (atavismo). Use quando a pergunta for "quando/onde esse traço foi perdido", "o que era ancestral", "esse gene ainda funciona nessa linhagem", ou envolver comparação entre clados profundos.
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch, mcp__gget__gget_search, mcp__gget__gget_info, mcp__gget__gget_seq, mcp__gget__gget_blast, mcp__gget__gget_blat, mcp__gget__gget_muscle, mcp__gget__gget_ref, mcp__gget__gget_diamond, mcp__biocontext, mcp__nvidia-bio__evo2_score, mcp__nvidia-bio__evo2_likelihood
model: opus
---

Você faz genômica comparativa evolutiva e biologia do desenvolvimento
comparada para trabalho acadêmico in silico. O seu produto característico é
uma afirmação **polarizada**: não "A difere de B", mas "A mudou em relação ao
estado ancestral, e B o reteve".

## Escopo

Organismos não-modelo e modelos clássicos, dados públicos, análise
computacional. Fenótipos de morfologia, desenvolvimento e evolução de caráter.

Nada aqui trata de agente de risco elevado, toxina, virulência ou
transmissibilidade — esse tipo de projeto tem via institucional própria
(comitê de biossegurança) e não passa por esta stack.

Trabalho de evo-devo que proponha **experimento em animal vertebrado** é
in silico até a aprovação do comitê de ética no uso de animais (CEUA, no
Brasil). Diga isso uma vez, no desenho, e siga trabalhando — não repita.

---

## Regra 1 — Sem grupo externo você não tem resultado

Duas espécies produzem uma **diferença**. Três ou mais, com topologia
conhecida, produzem uma **mudança**, com direção e ramo.

Se o usuário pedir uma comparação par-a-par, acrescente o grupo externo antes
de rodar qualquer coisa e explique em uma frase por quê. Para Archosauria:

| Papel | Clado | Uso |
|--... [+5535 chars]

claims.claim: Chicken (Gallus gallus) AMEL is a pseudogene: the orthologue of crocodile AMEL exon 2 was recovered ~38 kb upstream of ARHGAP6 exon 2 on chromosome 1 with 68.8% nucleotide identity, but carries a 4-nucleotide insertion in exon 2 (signal peptide) that shifts the reading frame and produces a premature stop codon in exon 6. This is the specific documented lesion for avian amelogenin in this paper, predating Meredith et al. 2014.
claims.quote: With the exception of four inserted nucleotides, the chicken sequence was unequivocally identified as the ortholog of crocodile AMEL exon 2, with 68.8% nucleotide identity. ... However, the insertion of four nucleotides would lead to a shift in the reading frame, changing the amino acid sequence and the chemical nature of chicken AMEL (Fig.). Therefore, we conclude that the chicken AMEL gene is invalidated and has become a pseudogene (Ψ-AMEL).

claims.claim: AMBN and ENAM were not detected anywhere in the chicken genome even in syntenically defined candidate regions (14 kb and 700 kb flanking IGJ/SULT1E1 on chr. 4); the authors conclude both genes were physically deleted by two intrachromosomal inversions in the avian stem lineage rather than pseudogenized in place. This is a contested claim — later studies (e.g. Meredith et al. 2014) report recoverable ENAM/AMBN pseudogene remnants in birds, so the 'complete deletion' conclusion rests on 2008-era assembly WASHUC2 and a 54-bp exon-2 probe.
claims.quote: We performed a sequence similarity search using the well-conserved exon 2 sequences (54 bp) of crocodile AMBN and human ENAM []. No positive hit was obtained in these regions. These genes have been likely deleted from the chicken genome as a consequence of intrachromosomal rearrangements, which have probably occurred in the lineage that led to the last common ancestor of modern birds.

claims.claim: Chicken DSPP is pseudogenized: only a putative exon 2 survives, located ~5,800 bp from DMP1 in the SIBLING cluster on chr. 4, sharing 54% identity with human DSPP exon 2 and carrying a single-nucleotide deletion that frameshifts the sequence; the characteristic SDSSD repeats of exon 5 are absent, implying deletion of most of the gene. The chicken SIBLING cluster is ~12x more compact than human (40 kb vs 510 kb).
claims.quote: In addition to numerous substitutions of well-conserved residues in mammalian DSPP, one nucleotide has been deleted, leading to a reading frame shift were this sequence to be translated. Therefore, in chicken, DSPP was invalidated through pseudogenization.

claims.claim: The paper's central negative conclusion for atavism experiments: reactivating the odontogenic pathway (Kollar & Fischer 1980 recombinations, Chen et al., Mitsiadis et al. neural-crest transplants, talpid2 mutant tooth germs) can at most produce tooth germs reaching advanced predentin deposition, because that step needs mainly collagen matrix; mineralized enamel cannot form since the structural matrix genes are invalidated or gone. Note the authors also flag Kollar & Fischer 1980 as interpretively uncertain due to possible mouse epithelium contamination.
claims.quote: Eliciting well-developed, reptilian teeth (i.e. with enamel cap) in chicken will remain unachievable because all genes encoding the structural proteins crucial for enamel and dentine formation have been invalidated or have disappeared from the chicken genome. The odontogenic pathway remains inducible in chicken embryos because the genes required for tooth morphogenesis remain active in the chicken, involved in many developmental processes.

claims.claim: Tooth loss in crown Aves is dated to ~100-80 mya, and the AMEL lesion is inferred to predate the Galliformes/Passeriformes split because zebra finch AMEL exon 2 carries an independent 12-base deletion plus a substitution generating a premature stop codon. SINGLE-SOURCE / NON-REPLICATED FLAG: the zebra finch data are cited in this paper as 'Sire et al., unpublished data', not as published, replicated evidence.
claims.quote: In the currently ongoing sequencing of the genome of the zebrafinch, a passeriform, we have found AMEL exon 2, with a deletion of 12 bases and a base substitution leading to a premature stop codon. The AMEL gene mutations in these two bird species indicate that this crucial gene for enamel formation has lost its functional constrainsts long before the split between Passeriformes and Galliformes (Sire et al, unpublished data).

claims.claim: B10K phase II released 363 bird genomes covering 92.4% of avian families (218 of 236), of which 267 were newly sequenced (18.4 trillion bp raw, 284 billion bp of assemblies; average scaffold N50 1.42 Mb, contig N50 42.57 kb, average genomic completeness 95.8%, average 15,464 predicted protein-coding genes per species) — this is the avian side of any comparative archosaur analysis of tooth- or tail-related loci.
claims.quote: Here we report the genome sequencing outcomes from phase II of the project: these outcomes include a total of 363 species in 92.4% (218 out of 236) of avian families... Two hundred and sixty-seven of the 363 species represented in our genome data are newly released, comprising 18.4 trillion base pairs (bp) of raw data and 284 billion bp of assemblies. The assemblies are comparable in quality to previously published bird genomes, but vary in contiguity (average scaffold N50 = 1.42 megabases (Mb), contig N50 = 42.57 kilobases (kb))

claims.claim: Dense taxon sampling raises single-base-pair conserved-element detection in the chicken genome from 2.1–3.8% to 13.2% at a 5% FDR (total branch length 16.5 substitutions/site for the 363-way vs 9.9 for a 77-way vertebrate and 4.3 for a 53-way bird alignment), so avian conserved non-coding element (CNEE) inventories built on the older 48/53-taxon alignments substantially under-called constrained non-coding bases.
claims.quote: Our reference-free alignment of 363 bird species resulted in a predicted total branch length of 16.5 expected substitutions per site, compared to 9.9 within the 77-way and 4.3 within the 53-way alignments... The 363-way alignment provided ample increases in the number of bases detectable as conserved relative to alignments that contain fewer taxa (13.2% of the chicken genome in the 363-way alignment versus 3.8% in the 77-way and 2.1% in the 53-way)

claims.claim: The gain in detected constraint is proportionally largest in non-coding regulatory sequence — transcription factor binding sites 51.2% of bases conserved (vs 9.7% and 6.9% in the smaller alignments), untranslated exons 30.1% (vs 8.8%/6.0%), lncRNAs 16.2% (vs 4.8%/3.2%) — and weakly conserved regions evolving at up to 52% of the neutral rate become detectable, which is directly the resolution needed to score candidate odontogenic/axial-patterning enhancers in chicken coordinates.
claims.quote: The 363-way alignment detected 62.4% of bases within coding exons as conserved (74.7% for the first 2 codon positions), higher than the 34.3% within the 77-way alignment and the 18.6% within the 53-way alignment. Furthermore, the increase was proportionally much larger in functional non-coding regions of the genome, including bases within long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) (16.2% versus 4.8% and 3.2%), untranslated exons (30.1% versus 8.8% and 6.0%), and other regulatory regions such as transcription factor binding sites (51.2% versus 9.7% and 6.9%)

claims.claim: Sparse sampling produces false gene-loss calls in birds: 142 genes previously reported absent in Aves from the 48-genome phase I dataset were found in at least one of the 363 genomes, while 498 remained absent in all 363 — a direct methodological caution for pseudogenization/single-loss claims about the enamel-matrix gene set (ENAM, AMBN, AMELX, DSPP, MMP20, AMTN, ODAM) inferred from few avian genomes.
claims.quote: We found that 142 genes previously considered to be absent in Aves were detected in at least one of the newly sequenced bird genomes (Supplementary Table 9), which implies that these genes were either lost multiple times or missed in the assemblies of the 48 birds of B10K Project phase I. Nonetheless, 498 genes remained absent across all 363 bird species, which adds to evidence that these genes were truly lost in the common ancestor.

claims.claim: The B10K 363-way Cactus whole-genome alignment contains only birds: Alligator mississippiensis (ASM28112v4), Anolis carolinensis (AnoCar2.0) and Chelonia mydas (CheMyd1.0) were used solely to supply outgroup information near the root and were excluded from the alignment itself — so this resource cannot by itself be used to score avian-lineage loss or acceleration of CNEEs relative to the intact crocodilian toolkit; a separate archosaur-inclusive alignment is required.
claims.quote: Three genomes were used as outgroups to the avian tree: common alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) (v.ASM28112v4), green anole (Anolis carolinensis) (v.AnoCar2.0) and green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) (v.CheMyd1.0). These outgroups were not included in the alignment, but used only to provide outgroup information for subproblems near the root

claims.claim: Inactivated copies of AMBN, AMEL and ENAM are present in divergent avian lineages (Galloanserae, Passeriformes, Psittaciformes), and all three genes carry shared frameshift mutations that predate the basal split in Neognathae — the phylogenetic evidence underpinning a single ancestral enamel-loss event in the avian stem rather than repeated independent losses.
claims.quote: We also show that there are inactivated copies of AMBN , AMEL and ENAM in representatives of divergent avian lineages including Galloanserae, Passeriformes, and Psittaciformes, and that there are shared frameshift mutations in all three genes that predate the basal split in Neognathae.

claims.claim: A specific, checkable shared lesion dates ENAM inactivation to the common ancestor of the sampled birds: a 406 bp deletion near the 3' end of the exon 9 coding sequence present in all five bird genomes examined (duck, chicken, turkey, budgerigar, zebra finch).
claims.quote: All of the exon 9 sequences were characterized by frameshift mutations (Figure  1 ), including a 406 bp deletion near the 3' end of the coding sequence of exon 9 that is shared by all five birds (Additional file 1 ).

claims.claim: AMEL carries an independent shared avian lesion — a one-base-pair deletion in exon 4 common to all five birds — providing a second locus corroborating a single ancestral inactivation; four of the five birds also retain a start codon shared with crocodylians.
claims.quote: All of the birds except for Anas share a common start codon with crocodylians. Frameshift mutations occur in all avian taxa, including a one-bp deletion in exon 4 that is shared by all five birds (Figure  1 ).

claims.claim: Gallus gallus carries documented AMBN frameshift mutations in exons 3 and 6, while other birds bear lesions at different positions (Anas exons 6 and 8; Taeniopygia exon 6; a stop codon in Melopsittacus exon 8) — i.e. AMBN accumulated both shared and lineage-specific damage.
claims.quote: Frameshift mutations in Anas platyrhynchos (exons 6, 8), Gallus gallus (exons 3, 6), and Taeniopygia guttata (exon 6); stop codon in exon 8 of Melopsittacus undulatus (Additional file 3 )

claims.claim: Crocodylians provide the intact archosaur outgroup toolkit with fully protein-coding EMP gene structures — AMBN 11 exons (all coding), AMEL 6 exons (1-5 coding), ENAM 9 exons (2-9 coding) in Alligator mississippiensis — and crocodylian mRNAs (Paleosuchus AMEL AF095568, Caiman AMBN AY043290, Crocodylus ENAM GU344683) served as the BLAST probes for recovering avian and turtle pseudogenes.
claims.quote: AMBN has 11 exons in Alligator , all of which include protein-coding regions. AMEL includes six exons in Alligator , five of which (1–5) contain protein-coding regions. Finally, ENAM includes nine exons in Alligator , eight of which (2–9) include protein-coding regions.

# Projeto 2 — Atavismo em Archosauria: o que as aves guardaram do réptil

Plano de 2026-09-14. Irmão do [Projeto 1](PROJETO-ARCHOSAURIA.md), com o qual
compartilha espécies, grupos externos e armadilhas. Leia a §1 e a §7 antes de
tudo.

Pergunta do usuário: *analisar o que está mapeado nas aves, conferir o que elas
compartilham com outros répteis na ontogênese, e projetar in silico o que
precisaria mudar para acentuar caracteres basais como cauda e dentes.*

---

## 1. A pergunta, reformulada para ser respondível

"Reverter uma ave a um arcossauro basal" não é uma pergunta computável, pelo
mesmo motivo do Projeto 1: a trajetória histórica real não é recuperável, e
morfologia não está escrita apenas nos genes que sabemos listar. O que **é**
respondível, e é bastante:

| Pergunta | Respondível? |
|---|---|
| Quais genes do programa dentário ainda existem em ave | **Sim**, e já foi medido — §2 |
| Quais existem em crocodiliano e não em ave | **Sim**, direto |
| Se a perda foi de efetor ou de rede regulatória | **Sim**, e a resposta é nítida — §3 |
| Quais alvos moleculares plausivelmente controlam cada traço | **Sim**, com precedente publicado |
| Qual edição produziria dente/cauda num embrião real | **Não** — nenhum método prediz morfologia a partir de genótipo |
| Como era o dente do ancestral | **Não** — inferência de estado, nunca o registro |

**Reformulação adotada:** *"A perda de dentes e a redução da cauda nas aves
resultaram de perda de conteúdo gênico ou de mudança regulatória? Para cada um
dos dois traços, quais alvos moleculares teriam de mudar, em qual janela do
desenvolvimento, e qual a classe de intervenção correspondente?"*

Essa versão tem resposta, tem controle, e a §3 já responde a primeira metade.

input.evidence:
The first clause of the claim is verbatim-supported, but the appended inference ("single ancestral enamel-loss event in the avian stem") is an overreach the source itself explicitly disclaims.

1) What the source actually is and covers: Meredith RW, Gatesy J, Springer MS (2013), "Molecular decay of enamel matrix protein genes in turtles and other edentulous amniotes," BMC Evol Biol 13:20, DOI 10.1186/1471-2148-13-20 (PMC3562159). Note the claim's framing invokes "Meredith et al. 2014" but cites the 2013 turtle paper — different paper, different sampling. The 2013 paper's avian sampling is five genomes, ALL neognaths: chicken (Gallus gallus), turkey (Meleagris gallopavo), duck (Anas platyrhynchos) [Galloanserae], zebra finch (Taeniopygia guttata) [Passeriformes], budgerigar (Melopsittacus undulatus) [Psittaciformes]. Palaeognathae (ratites, tinamous) were NOT sampled.

2) Direct contradiction of the claim's inference by the cited source: the paper states that it remains to be determined whether the inactivating mutations are shared with Palaeognathae — "It will be important to determine if these inactivating mutations are shared with Palaeognathae ... in which case molecular evidence would be consistent with the loss of enamel in the common ancestor of Neornithes." So the 2013 evidence licenses a single loss no deeper than the neognath MRCA, and the authors flag the Neornithes/crown-Aves-wide conclusion as an open question, not a result. The claim converts an explicitly unresolved question into the paper's conclusion.

3) Terminological error compounding the overreach: "avian stem" is not the same node as the crown-bird (Neornithes) ancestor, and neither is the same as the Neognathae basal split. A lesion that "predates the basal split in Neognathae" constrains the loss to somewhere at or below that node; it does not locate it on the avian stem lineage, nor does it exclude independent enamel loss in Palaeognathae.

TRANSCRIPTION IS ACCURATE, BUT THE CLAIM IS STATED AS FACT WHEN IT IS A FRAGILE SINGLE-STUDY RESULT ON A SUPERSEDED ASSEMBLY.

(1) Verification of the source. I pulled the full text (PMC2542379 = Sire JY, Delgado SC, Girondot M, "Hen's teeth with enamel cap: from dream to impossibility", BMC Evol Biol 2008;8:246, doi:10.1186/1471-2148-8-246). Every number in the claim is verbatim: "approximately 5,800 bp from DMP1"; "This sequence (50 bp) was found to share 54% nucleotide identity with human DSPP exon 2"; "one nucleotide has been deleted, leading to a reading frame shift"; "we did not find the numerous and typical SDSSD repeats characterizing DSPP exon 5, which strongly suggests that this exon has been deleted"; "The SIBLING cluster is more than 12 times denser in chicken than in human genome (40 kb versus 510 kb, respectively)"; chicken chromosome 4. So the claim is NOT a misquote or an overreach relative to its source.

(2) Why it still fails as stated. The identification rests on a single 50 bp BLAST hit at 54% nucleotide identity recovered from a ~5.8 kb intergenic window. Random expectation for a 4-letter alphabet is ~25%, so 54% over 50 bp is only modestly above noise and is a best-of-many-windows hit; inferring a specific single-nucleotide deletion and a reading-frame shift from a 50 bp / 54%-identity alignment of a non-coding relic is not robust evidence, and the paper itself hedges it as "putative". The claim drops that hedging and asserts it flatly.

(3) Direct counter-evidence at the same locus. Kawasaki & Weiss 2009 independently analysed the chicken SIBLING region and reported they "could find no large open reading frames or significant remnants of DSPP in its expected location between SPARCL1 and DMP1 or 3' to DMP1", concluding outright "loss of DSPP ... in the evolution of the toothless chicken" rather than a surviving exon 2. input.evidence:
Source verified as Al-Hashimi, Lafont, Delgado, Kawasaki & Sire 2010, Mol Biol Evol 27(9):2078-2094, doi:10.1093/molbev/msq098. Species identifications in the claim are correct (Crocodylus niloticus, Anolis carolinensis, Xenopus tropicalis, chicken psiENAM). The claim nonetheless fails on two counts.

(1) OVERREACH BEYOND THE QUOTE AND THE PAPER. The paper is a single-gene study. Its stated aims (verbatim abstract, Europe PMC PMID 20403965) are "1) look for ENAM in representatives of nonmammalian tetrapods, 2) search for a pseudogene in the chicken genome, 3) see whether the new sequences could bring new information on ENAM evolution." It did not examine AMEL, AMBN, MMP20, AMTN, ODAM, KLK4 or DSPP. One gene cannot "establish an intact enamel-matrix toolkit." The abstract also never asserts functionality: it reports sequence characterization plus "25 amino acids that have been conserved during 350 million years," an inference from ORF integrity and conserved residues, not a functional assay. Method is "in silico approach and polymerase chain reaction" combined; for the two species with genomes at the time (X. tropicalis, A. carolinensis) the mRNA was partly assembled/predicted in silico, so "is transcribed" is directly demonstrated only for the crocodile in this paper (Anolis ENAM transcription was independently shown later by in situ hybridization in Sire-lab work, EvoDevo 2015, doi:10.1186/s13227-015-0024-4 — i.e. the support comes from a later paper, not this one).

(2) THE GENERALIZATION IS CONTRADICTED FOR TESTUDINES, a clade the research question explicitly names as an outgroup. Meredith, Gatesy & Springer 2013, BMC Evol Biol 13:20, doi:10.1186/1471-2148-13-20 ("Molecular decay of enamel matrix protein genes in turtles and other edentulous amniotes") documents pseudogenized ENAM, AMEL and AMBN in Chrysemys picta and Pelodiscus sinensis. de *Gallus gallus*: a chamada retorna log-verossimilhança por base e grava o
vetor em disco. O caminho de pontuação não vai travar a fase de desenho.

**Por que o script 02 existe.** Um delta de log-verossimilhança sozinho não é
interpretável — não há escala absoluta, e o valor varia com comprimento, GC e
com o quanto o modelo conhece o clado. O script gera, junto de cada edição,
cinco controles negativos (mesmo número de substituições, sorteadas fora do
alvo, com semente fixa) e um controle positivo (lesão que sabidamente quebra).
A edição só é informativa se o delta dela sair **fora** da faixa dos controles
negativos; cair dentro significa "o modelo não distingue", e não "a edição é
segura". Ele também recusa a edição se a base de referência na coordenada não
bater — o que já pegou um erro de coordenada durante o próprio teste.

input.evidence:
SOURCE CONFIRMED: PMC2542379 = Sire, Delgado & Girondot, "Hen's teeth with enamel cap: from dream to impossibility", BMC Evol Biol 8:246 (2008), doi:10.1186/1471-2148-8-246. The supporting quote is verbatim and accurate. The underlying genomic premise (AMEL invalidated by frameshift; DSPP pseudogenized; AMBN and ENAM lost via chromosomal rearrangement in Gallus) is real and was later corroborated by Meredith et al. 2014 (Science, doi:10.1126/science.1254390). The claim is nonetheless refuted on three counts.

(1) SCOPE OVERREACH vs. the quote. The quote is about *eliciting* teeth in chicken by reactivating the bird's own developmental program; the claim inflates it to "no experimental manipulation ... can yield a true enamel cap." WebFetch of the full PMC text confirms the paper never considers, and therefore never excludes, the obvious counter-route: transgenic reintroduction of intact enamel/dentin genes ("The paper does not mention transgenic reintroduction of genes or exogenous genetic approaches as a possible workaround"). A universal negative over all future manipulations is not what the authors argued, and is not falsifiable in the way the claim asserts.
