findings.claim: Mineralized teeth were lost once, in the common ancestor of modern birds (Neornithes), evidenced by inactivating mutations in enamel- and dentin-expressed genes shared across lineages of nearly all extant bird orders.
sources: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1254390 (Meredith RW, Zhang G, Gilbert MTP, Jarvis ED, Springer MS, Science 346(6215):1254390, 2014, doi:10.1126/science.1254390, PMID 25504730)
https://bmcecolevol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2148-13-20 (Meredith RW, Gatesy J, Springer MS, BMC Evol Biol 13:20, 2013, doi:10.1186/1471-2148-13-20)
findings.evidence: Verbatim abstract: 'We performed comparative genomic analyses representing lineages of nearly all extant bird orders and recovered shared, inactivating mutations within genes expressed in both the enamel and dentin of teeth of other vertebrate species, indicating that the common ancestor of modern birds lacked mineralized teeth.' Sample = the 48-genome Jarvis et al. 2014 avian phylogenomics dataset. The inference rests on present-but-lesioned orthologues carrying shared frameshifts/stops, NOT on gene absence, so it is immune to the avian 'false gene loss' artefact literature (Bornelov 2017; Hron 2018; Kim 2022 doi:10.1186/s13059-022-02765-0) that plagues GC-rich microchromosome calls in short-read bird assemblies. No published technical comment, eLetter or reanalysis arguing convergent within-crown loss was located in 12 years. THREE SCOPE LIMITS THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE CLAIM: (a) the authors hedge the phenotype themselves - 'tooth loss, OR AT LEAST the loss of enamel caps' - so single-loss is demonstrated for mineralized teeth/enamel, and total edentulism could have been staged; (b) the statement applies to CROWN birds only: among Mesozoic stem birds tooth loss was repeatedly and independently acquired (Confuciusornis, Gobipteryx, Archaeorhynchus, Schizooura; Brocklehurst & Field 2021, PMC7973866) and toothed ornithurines (Hesperornis, Ichthyornis) persisted to the end-Cretaceous; restating this loosely as 'birds lost teeth only once' IS an overreach; (c) the 2013 precursor paper's shared 406 bp ENAM exon-9 deletion strictly dates only to the Neognathae node, and the authors explicitly flagged that palaeognath sampling was needed - which the 2014 48-genome paper then supplied.

findings.claim: The avian tooth-loss event is dated to ~116 Ma by Meredith et al., but that number is contested downstream and should be cited as an attribution rather than as settled fact.
sources: Brocklehurst N, Field DJ, iScience 2021, PMC7973866 (macroevolutionary dynamics of dentition in Mesozoic birds)
findings.evidence: Verbatim: 'We estimate that tooth loss, or at least the loss of enamel caps that provide the outer layer of mineralized teeth, occurred about 116 million years ago.' The dating is selection-relaxation / frameshift-accumulation dating on the pseudogenes placed on the modern-bird stem branch, not a fossil-calibrated node age - so the research prompt's phrase 'dating of the lesions' is loose but not a misread. CONTESTED: Brocklehurst & Field 2021 state directly 'Both of these are substantially younger than previous estimates (116 mya [Meredith et al., 2014a])' and report a median ~88-90 Ma for the transition to full edentulism. The 116 Ma figure is also contingent on the Jarvis et al. 2014 timetree, since revised (Prum et al. 2015; Stiller et al. 2024 Nature). Additionally, the widely-cited '~60 Myr' figure from Chen et al. 2000 is an outdated lower bound and should not be used; cite ~116 Ma (Meredith) or >=66 Ma (fossil record) with the ~88-90 Ma counter-estimate. The split vote reflects the contested number, not doubt about the attribution.

findings.claim: Specific, editable lesions are documented in Gallus gallus for AMEL, DSPP and ENAM - these are the concrete coordinates any in-silico reversion design would target.
findings.vote: 3-0 (AMEL), 2-1 (DSPP), 3-0 (ENAM)
sources: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1471-2148-8-246 (Sire JY, Delgado SC, Girondot M, 'Hen's teeth with enamel cap: from dream to impossibility', BMC Evol Biol 8:246, 2008, doi:10.1186/1471-2148-8-246, PMC2542379, PMID 18775069)
https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/27/9/2078/1009898 (Al-Hashimi N, Lafont AG, Delgado S, Kawasaki K, Sire JY, Mol Biol Evol 27(9):2078-2094, 2010, doi:10.1093/molbev/msq098, PMID 20403965)
findings.evidence: AMEL (psi-AMEL): orthologue of crocodile AMEL exon 2 recovered ~38 kb upstream of ARHGAP6 exon 2 on chicken chr. 1, 68.8% nucleotide identity; a 4-nucleotide insertion in exon 2 (signal peptide) shifts the reading frame and yields a premature stop codon in exon 6. Caveats: the 4-nt insertion is causative but not the only lesion (further indels in exon 3 and both ends of exon 6; exons 1 and 4 never recovered); the finding is purely in silico from WASHUC2/galGal3 with no PCR/Sanger validation reported; the 'crocodile' comparator is GenBank AF095568 from Paleosuchus palpebrosus, NOT Alligator mississippiensis, and should be named by species. DSPP: only a putative exon 2 survives, ~5,800 bp from DMP1 in the SIBLING cluster on chr. 4, 54% identity to human DSPP exon 2 over a ~50 bp manually aligned window, carrying a single-nucleotide deletion that frameshifts; the characteristic SDSSD repeats of exon 5 are absent ('strongly suggests that this exon has been deleted'). The chicken SIBLING cluster is >12x more compact than human (40 kb vs 510 kb). Chromosome assignment still holds on a current assembly: ENSGALG00010002428 (IBSP/DMP1 locus) is on seq_region 4 at 45,249,489-45,255,379 in bGalGal1.mat.broiler.GRCg7b. Report the fragment length with the 54% figure and flag exon-5 'deletion' as an argument from absence, not an observed breakpoint. ENAM: 'All of the exon 9 sequences were characterized by frameshift mutations ... including a 406 bp deletion near the 3' end of the coding sequence of exon 9 that is shared by all five birds' - positions 3353-3758, taxa Gallus gallus, Meleagris gallopavo, Anas platyrhynchos, Melopsittacus undulatus, Taeniopygia guttata, alignment deposited as Additional file 1, so the lesion is literally checkable. A shared deletion sets a MINIMUM age for that lesion (Neognathae node); read dates as 'no later than'.

findings.claim: The 2008 conclusion that AMBN and ENAM were physically deleted from the chicken genome was self-corrected in 2010: chicken psi-ENAM exists, located off-synteny on chromosome Z. This is a methodological warning, not just a historical footnote.
findings.evidence: Sire et al. 2008 searched two syntenically-defined candidate regions (14 kb and 700 kb, flanking IGJ/SULT1E1 on chr. 4) plus a genome-wide BLASTN using only the 54 bp exon-2 probes of crocodile AMBN and human ENAM: 'No positive hit was obtained in these regions. These genes have been likely deleted from the chicken genome as a consequence of intrachromosomal rearrangements'. Two inversions were identified in the IGJ-adjacent region. Al-Hashimi et al. 2010 - same senior author - then recovered chicken psi-ENAM by in silico search PLUS PCR, on chromosome Z downstream of LPL and upstream of NRG1/FUT10, i.e. entirely outside the mammal-synteny-guided search space, interpreted as a sauropsid-lineage translocation. Abstract: 'search for a pseudogene in the chicken genome ... we obtained and characterized ... the putative sequence of chicken ENAM pseudogene', concluding 'tooth loss in modern birds led to the invalidation of enamel genes'. TWO OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCES: (1) synteny-guided absence calls on 2008-era assemblies are unreliable - the enamelin locus persists as a degraded relic rather than being deleted outright; (2) AMBN remains the weakest link: Sire 2008 reports it absent, and 'recoverable AMBN remnants in birds' was NOT independently verified in this pass (several summaries of Meredith 2014 list the shared lesions as DSPP + ENAM/AMELX/AMTN/MMP20 without AMBN). Do not assert AMBN status without re-deriving it. All lesion coordinates should be re-mapped onto GRCg6a/GRCg7b/bGalGal1 before entering a methods section; the authors' own 2010 hedge 'putative' should also be preserved.

findings.claim: The non-avian sauropsid outgroup retains a functional enamel-matrix toolkit: ENAM mRNA is transcribed and intact in crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus), lizard (Anolis carolinensis) and frog (Xenopus tropicalis) - but the verified evidence covers ONE gene, not the whole toolkit.
sources: Gasse et al. on amelotin in Alligator mississippiensis and Caiman crocodilus, PMC4373244
findings.evidence: Al-Hashimi 2010 recovered ENAM mRNA coding sequence for all three species (crocodile and lizard exon 4 to exon 10; frog full-length except the middle of the large exon 10), each a single isoform with intact signal peptide and conserved functional residues (3 putative phosphoserines, 3 N-glycosylation asparagines, 6 cysteines). Independently corroborated: Chen/Sire et al. 2015 EvoDevo demonstrated ENAM (with AMEL, AMBN, AMTN) actually expressed in Anolis carolinensis ameloblasts during amelogenesis - the first such demonstration in a non-mammal. OVERREACH FLAG: the phrase 'intact enamel-matrix toolkit' generalizes beyond the single gene this source establishes. AMELX/AMBN/AMTN/ODAM/MMP20/KLK4/DSPP intactness in these outgroups must be cited to Meredith et al. 2013 BMC Evol Biol 13:20, Sire et al. 2015 EvoDevo 6:23, and Gasse et al. on AMTN - not to Al-Hashimi 2010. Also note Xenopus tropicalis is an amphibian outgroup to Amniota, not a sauropsid, and its exon-10 interior was not fully sequenced, so 'functional' there rests on the recovered transcript plus conserved motifs rather than a complete ORF. For a donor-sequence design, the crocodilian orthologues are the phylogenetically appropriate source; verify each gene individually rather than assuming toolkit-wide intactness.

findings.claim: The upstream odontogenic regulatory network is NOT lost in birds: FGF8, PITX2, BARX1 and PAX9 are expressed in the chick mandible and demarcate a potential odontogenic region positionally equivalent to the mouse dental lamina, and a chick oral rudiment resembling the lamina stage of the mammalian molar germ does form. Avian tooth development is arrested early, not absent from the outset.
findings.vote: 3-0 (regulators), 2-1 (rudiment)
sources: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.160245097 (Chen Y, Zhang Y, Jiang TX, Barlow AJ, St Amand TR, Hu Y, Heaney S, Francis-West P, Chuong CM, Maas R, 'Conservation of early odontogenic signaling pathways in Aves', PNAS 97(18):10044-9, 2000, doi:10.1073/pnas.160245097, PMID 10954731, PMC27667)
Lainoff AJ, Moustakas-Verho JE, Hu D, Kallonen A, Marcucio RS, Hlusko LJ, J Exp Zool B 324(3):255-69, 2015, doi:10.1002/jez.b.22594, PMC4401653
Louryan S et al., J Morphol 283(2):207-18, 2021, doi:10.1002/jmor.21437
findings.evidence: Verbatim abstract: 'Similar to the mouse dental lamina, expression of Fgf8, Pitx2, Barx1, and Pax9 defines a potential chick odontogenic region' and 'in the chick oral cavity a rudiment forms that resembles the lamina stage of the mammalian molar tooth germ'. NOT a single-study claim: chick Barx1 craniofacial expression (Barlow et al.) and chick Fgf8 mandibular-epithelium expression are independently established; Lainoff 2015 reports conserved Pitx2, Pax9 and Barx1 expression in the independently edentulous turtle Trachemys scripta; Louryan 2021 reports SHH, BMP4, PITX2 and PAX9 in parrot beak epithelium and mesenchyme with high-level clusters in pseudotooth rudiments - a second bird family, 21 years later. TWO WORDING CORRECTIONS FOR ANY WRITE-UP: (1) downgrade 'homologous to the mouse dental lamina' to 'similar to / positionally equivalent to' - the paper says 'similar', and 'resembles', not formal homology; (2) MANDATORY PAIRING - the very next sentence of the same abstract states 'the expression of three molecules involved in tooth initiation, Bmp4, Msx1, and Msx2, are absent from the presumptive chick dental lamina'. Quoting the four retained regulators without the three absent ones would falsely imply an end-to-end intact cascade. (Note: the standalone claim about the three absent genes did not itself survive the verification vote (0-3), so cite it from the primary abstract directly rather than as an independently verified finding.) Also note the research prompt miscites Chen et al. 2000 as 'Development'; it is PNAS.

findings.claim: The latent chick odontogenic cascade is experimentally re-inducible: exogenous BMP restores Msx expression in chick mandibles and BMP+FGF promotes development of Sonic hedgehog-expressing epithelial structures - but what is recovered is Shh-positive epithelial structures/appendages of ambiguous tooth-vs-feather identity, never mineralized teeth.
findings.evidence: Verbatim: 'In chick mandibles, exogenous bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) induces Msx expression and together with fibroblast growth factor promotes the development of Sonic hedgehog expressing epithelial structures'; and 'Distinct epithelial appendages also were induced when chick mandibular epithelium was recombined with a tissue source of BMPs and fibroblast growth factors, chick skin mesenchyme'. The authors' own conclusion: 'although latent, the early signaling pathways involved in odontogenesis remain inducible in Aves'. CRITICAL SELF-LIMITATION in the full text (PMC27667): 'The present work suggests that in Aves early steps in the odontogenic pathway potentially exist in latent form. It does not, however, demonstrate the formation in Aves of structures that can be called teeth.' No mineralization was reported; the induced structures 'were not typical tooth or feather germs, but exhibited some morphologic features consistent with both fates'. Method note: these were recombinant-protein beads and tissue recombination, not small-molecule pharmacology - 'pharmacologically inducible' is loose. Importantly, this is an ALL-AVIAN induction (chick epithelium + chick skin mesenchyme), which means early odontogenic signalling CAN be initiated in birds without heterologous mesenchyme, even though no tooth results.

findings.claim: The Chen et al. 2000 proposal that loss of odontogenic Bmp4 expression is the specific cause of early arrest of avian tooth development is a single-node causal hypothesis that has never been independently confirmed, and a competing positional/epigenetic model exists.
sources: Harris MP, Hasso SM, Ferguson MWJ, Fallon JF, Curr Biol 16(4):371-7, 2006, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2005.12.047, PMID 16488870
Lainoff AJ et al., J Exp Zool B 324(3):255-69, 2015, doi:10.1002/jez.b.22594
findings.evidence: The paper's own wording is hedged - 'suggest that loss of odontogenic Bmp4 expression MAY BE responsible for the early arrest of tooth development in living birds' - and any downstream text must preserve 'proposed', not 'showed'. Three independent pressures on the hypothesis: (1) Lainoff et al. 2015 show the Bmp4 domain is also proximally limited in the TOOTHED opossum Monodelphis domestica and the Fgf8 domain distally limited in the TOOTHED alligator, concluding that 'a limited Bmp4 domain does not necessarily correlate with edentulism' and that odontogenesis initiation in non-murine amniotes is 'more complex than previously imagined'; (2) Harris et al. 2006 propose instead an epigenetic/positional model in which a lateral signalling centre is displaced relative to competent odontogenic mesenchyme, and recapitulate early talpid2 events via beta-catenin activation rather than by restoring Bmp4; (3) regulatory restoration of Bmp4 could not in any case restore enamel, given the shared inactivating frameshifts in the matrix genes predating the Neognathae split. The four-gene expression observation (finding above) is NOT contested; only this causal node is. NOTE: the related standalone claims about Harris et al. 2006 - that talpid2 teeth were 'archosaurian/crocodilian first-generation teeth', that beta-catenin activation in wild-type chicks reproduced the talpid2 early events, and the lateral-signalling-centre model - all FAILED the verification vote (0-3, 1-2, 0-3) and must be treated as unverified in this pass, even though they are referenced second-hand in the sources above.

findings.claim: The hard ceiling on avian dental atavism BY REACTIVATION: because the structural matrix genes are invalidated or gone, reactivated tooth germs can at most reach advanced predentin deposition (a step requiring mainly collagen matrix); an enamel cap is unachievable. This is a theoretical prediction from gene content, never experimentally demonstrated, and it does NOT exclude transgenic reintroduction.
findings.evidence: Verbatim: 'Eliciting well-developed, reptilian teeth (i.e. with enamel cap) in chicken will remain unachievable because all genes encoding the structural proteins crucial for enamel and dentine formation have been invalidated or have disappeared from the chicken genome. The odontogenic pathway remains inducible in chicken embryos because the genes required for tooth morphogenesis remain active in the chicken, involved in many developmental processes.' And: 'tooth germs that form with experimental reactivation of this pathway or in ta2 chicken mutants could develop until an advanced stage of predentin deposition because the process to this point requires mainly collagen matrix deposition.' FOUR QUALIFICATIONS THAT NARROW BUT DO NOT REFUTE IT, all directly relevant to an in-silico design: (a) SCOPE - the impossibility applies to atavism-by-reactivation of the ENDOGENOUS chicken program; it says nothing about, and does not exclude, transgenic/knock-in reintroduction of functional enamel-matrix genes. Presenting this as 'enamel in birds is impossible, full stop' is an overreach. (b) PREDICTION, NOT OBSERVATION - the predentin ceiling was never experimentally reached; the authors note 'the oldest ta2 died at stages E16' and explicitly leave open whether teeth with an enamel cap would have been obtained 'under different experimental conditions or if the chicken mutants had survived'. Flag as non-replicated at the experimental level. (c) GENE COVERAGE - Sire 2008 analysed only four genes (AMEL, DSPP, AMBN, ENAM); MMP20, AMTN and ODAM come from Meredith 2013/2014 and Springer et al. 2019 (ODAM, BMC Evol Biol, doi:10.1186/s12862-019-1359-6). Cite the lesion inventory from Meredith, not Sire. (d) Preserve Sire's two-mechanism distinction 'invalidated OR gone' (pseudogenization vs deletion); do not collapse it to 'pseudogenized'.

findings.claim: Pre-2006, no experiment had initiated tooth development de novo in an all-avian system; avian epidermis had been shown to participate in tooth formation only when recombined with heterologous (mouse or lizard) odontogenic mesenchyme. Of that recombination lineage, Kollar & Fisher 1980 is interpretively contested; Mitsiadis et al. 2003 is not.
sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982206000649 (Harris MP, Hasso SM, Ferguson MWJ, Fallon JF, 'The Development of Archosaurian First-Generation Teeth in a Chicken Mutant', Curr Biol 16:371-377, 2006, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2005.12.047)
findings.evidence: Verbatim from Harris et al. 2006: 'Although recombination studies have shown that the avian epidermis can respond to tooth-inductive cues from mouse or lizard oral mesenchyme and participate in tooth formation, attempts to initiate tooth development de novo in birds have failed.' Sire et al. 2008 independently concur that no experiment achieved differentiated avian teeth, and on Kollar & Fisher specifically: 'In 1980, Kollar and Fischer recombined chick dental epithelium with mouse mesenchyme and obtained teeth with an enamel cover, the famous "hen's teeth." ... However, a possible contamination of the mouse mesenchyme by mouse epithelium makes the interpretation uncertain.' TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) Do NOT lump Mitsiadis et al. 2003 with Kollar & Fisher under 'contested' - the same review treats Mitsiadis favourably ('showed that avian dental epithelium can still induce a nonavian developmental program in mouse neural crest-derived mesenchyme, resulting in tooth germ formation'). 'Non-de-novo' applies to both; 'contested' applies only to Kollar & Fisher 1980. (2) The absolute 'only with heterologous mesenchyme' is too strong at the level of early odontogenic SIGNALLING: Chen et al. 2000 ran all-avian experiments (BMP/FGF induction of Shh-expressing buds; chick mandibular epithelium + chick skin mesenchyme) that initiated odontogenic signalling without heterologous tissue - yielding epithelial buds/appendages, never teeth. Note also that the framing sentence is an introduction claim by the talpid2 authors themselves (partly self-serving), though corroborated by the independent Sire 2008 review; and the talpid2 result itself is a single mutant line (later tied to C2CD3, Chang et al. 2014) carrying its own replication caveat.

input.caveats: COVERAGE IS THE BIGGEST CAVEAT. Only sections (1) and (2) of the six-part research question are actually answered by surviving claims. NOTHING survived on: section (3) axial elongation and tail termination (GDF11, LIN28A/let-7, CDX, HOX13 paralogs, WNT3A, FGF8/RA gradients, TBXT/Brachyury including Xia et al. 2024 Nature, pygostyle formation, avian tail-bud apoptosis, Rashid et al. 2014 EvoDevo, Archaeopteryx/Caudipteryx caudal counts); section (4) comparative archosaur genomics beyond the single ENAM gene (crocodilian genomes as outgroup, polyphyodonty and the crocodilian dental lamina, CNEEs lost/accelerated in the avian stem, B10K, HH-vs-crocodilian stage correspondence); section (5) in-silico methodology (Evo 2 / Nucleotide Transformer / DNABERT-2 variant-effect scoring and its validated limits in non-human vertebrates, CRISPR/base/prime editing in chicken PGCs, chicken ATAC-seq/ChIP-seq enhancer atlases, folding intrinsically disordered enamel-matrix proteins); section (6) ethics, welfare, regulatory framing and the "dino-chicken" spectacle critique. Treat those as UNANSWERED, not as answered negatively — a second research pass is required before the tail half of the project has any evidentiary basis. SECOND: eleven claims were voted refuted, and inspection shows most failed on attribution/overreach wording rather than on being factually false — notably three Harris et al. 2006 talpid2 claims (archosaurian/crocodilian first-generation teeth, beta-catenin sufficiency, the lateral-signalling-centre model) and several Meredith 2013 lesion-inventory claims (AMEL exon-4 1-bp deletion; AMBN exon-3/6 frameshifts in Gallus). Do not cite those as verified, and do not cite them as disproved either; re-verify them directly against the primary texts if they are to be load-bearing. THIRD: assembly currency. Every coordinate above (chr. 1 AMEL/ARHGAP6, chr. 4 DSPP/SIBLING, chr. Z ENAM, ENAM exon 9 positions 3353-3758) derives from WASHUC2/galGal3 (2008) or 2011-2012 short-re... [+1251 chars]
openQuestions: What is the genetic basis of avian tail termination and the pygostyle — is it gene loss (as with the enamel matrix) or purely regulatory/heterochronic? Nothing on GDF11, CDX, HOX13, TBXT, LIN28A/let-7, WNT3A, tail-bud apoptosis or caudal somite counts survived this pass, so it is currently unknown whether the two target traits (teeth and tail) have the same class of molecular lesion — which determines whether a single design strategy can address both.

Is AMBN present as a recoverable relic in Gallus or genuinely deleted? Sire 2008 reports absence, the 2010 psi-ENAM discovery discredits the synteny-guided method that produced that absence call, and AMBN was the one gene not independently confirmed in the shared-lesion inventory. This must be settled against GRCg7b before an enamel-matrix restoration set can be specified.

Given that atavism-by-reactivation is capped at predentin, what would a minimal transgenic complement actually be — which crocodilian orthologues (AMEL, AMBN, ENAM, AMTN, ODAM, MMP20, KLK4, DSPP) are jointly necessary and sufficient for enamel deposition, and is there any published knock-in evidence in any system that reintroducing matrix genes into an edentulous background restores mineralization?

How well do genomic language models (Evo 2, Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2) actually perform on non-mammalian vertebrate regulatory and variant-effect scoring, and are they validated at all on avian genomes? This is the core methodological question for the project's in-silico scoring plan and no evidence on it was returned.

Where does the institutional line sit between a defensible evo-devo experiment and the "dino-chicken" spectacle framing, and what animal-ethics review path applies to germline-transgenic galliformes? Given the project's own CLAUDE.md routing of elevated-risk work to the biosafety committee, this needs an explicit answer before any wet-lab framing is written.

input.question: Genetic and developmental basis of tail reduction in birds (pygostyle formation, caudal somite loss, axial elongation termination), the in-silico methods to model reversing it, whether avian tail reduction is gene loss or regulatory change, the hominoid TBXT/AluY precedent, and the ethics/feasibility of germline work in chicken.
input.summary: The question has one decisive fork (is tail reduction loss-of-gene or loss/change-of-regulation, i.e. the same class of problem as avian tooth loss or not?) sitting on top of three evidence layers: avian-specific descriptive embryology, amniote axial-termination genetics that is overwhelmingly mouse-derived, and a validated single-lesion precedent in hominoids. I split the search so that each layer is probed separately — avian tail program, mouse-vs-chick termination mechanism, hominoid TBXT precedent, avian-lineage comparative genomics (gene loss / CNE loss / accelerated elements), model-and-data validity for non-mammalian vertebrates, and the wet-lab/ethics path — so that an absence of avian evidence in any layer shows up as an explicit gap rather than being masked by abundant mouse literature.

angles.label: Avian tail program (primary embryology)
angles.query: chicken pygostyle development caudal somite number tail bud apoptosis Hamburger-Hamilton axial elongation Archaeopteryx Caudipteryx Rashid 2014 EvoDevo "tail of evolution"
angles.rationale: Establishes the descriptive baseline in Gallus: how many caudal somites form versus Alligator/Archaeopteryx/Caudipteryx, whether distal somites are cleared by programmed cell death, at which HH stage elongation stops, and what the Rashid review demonstrates versus merely proposes.

angles.label: Axial termination mechanism, mouse vs chick
angles.query: axial elongation termination tailbud Gdf11 null homeotic Lin28a let-7 Cdx dosage Hoxb13 null long tail Wnt3a vestigial tail Fgf8 retinoic acid wavefront neuromesodermal progenitors chick embryo
angles.rationale: Pulls the mechanistic gene set (GDF11, LIN28/let-7, CDX, HOX13, WNT3A, FGF8/RA, TBXT) together with any chick-embryo work, so the mouse-to-bird transfer gap can be flagged gene by gene instead of assumed.

angles.label: Hominoid single-lesion precedent
angles.query: Xia 2024 Nature TBXT AluY insertion exon skipping hominoid tail loss mouse model neural tube defects 10.1038/s41586-024-07095-8
angles.rationale: Nails down exactly what was shown (species, allele, model organism, phenotype penetrance) and the neural-tube-defect cost, which is the hard design constraint on any engineered tail-lengthening allele.

angles.label: Gene loss vs regulatory change in the avian stem lineage
angles.query: avian genome gene loss pseudogenization conserved non-coding element loss avian-accelerated regulatory elements bird stem lineage axial caudal developmental genes comparative genomics
angles.rationale: The decisive question: whether any published comparative-genomics work links loss of genes or conserved/accelerated CNEs to the avian axial program. A well-searched null result here is itself the answer and separates tail from teeth.

angles.label: In-silico model and data validity outside mammals

angles.rationale: Tests whether the modelling tools and the chicken enhancer/accessibility resources they would be applied to are actually validated on avian sequence, and surfaces the assembly-version caveat for any coordinate-level claim.

angles.rationale: Covers what is genuinely routine in chicken PGC germline engineering, the applicable animal-ethics/biosafety review route, and peer-reviewed criticism of the dino-chicken framing that marks the line between evo-devo experiment and spectacle.

results.title: Genome Editing in the Chicken: From PGC-Mediated Germline Transmission to Advanced Applications (He et al. 2025, Int J Mol Sci 26:9426; PMC12524394)
results.snippet: Directly answers question (5)'s wet-lab half: the most current peer-reviewed review of what is actually routine in chicken germline engineering. Establishes that avian editing lagged mammals because pronuclear injection is impossible in a telolecithal egg, and that the enabling breakthrough was long-term in vitro culture of primordial germ cells (PGCs), which made the chicken 'a tractable and powerful model for genetic engineering.' Chronicles the path from untargeted transgenesis to CRISPR knock-in/knockout and flags 'emerging precision editors' (base/prime) as still-emerging rather than established in birds — i.e. for a tail project, knockout and knock-in at a PGC locus are routine; a precise regulatory-element edit (the AluY/TBXT-style lesion of question 3) is not yet demonstrated germline in chicken. Note the applications surveyed are all agricultural/biomedical (disease resistance, oviduct bioreactors, surrogate hosts) — no morphological/evo-devo atavism line is cited, which is itself evidence about where the field puts its justification.

results.title: Germline Gene Editing in Chickens by Efficient CRISPR-Mediated Homologous Recombination in Primordial Germ Cells (Dimitrov et al. 2016, PLoS ONE 11:e0154303; PMC4839619)
results.snippet: The founding demonstration that CRISPR germline editing works in chicken, and the citation that turns 'could you edit a chicken?' into a settled yes. gRNA plus HDR donor co-transfected into cultured PGCs, clonal selection, 100% of drug-resistant clones carried the correct targeting event, and the targeted PGCs gave healthy germline-transmitting progeny. Important caveat for a tail project: the target was the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus — a biotech antibody-platform locus, selectable in vitro. Nothing about this result transfers automatically to editing an axial-patterning enhancer, where there is no drug selection and the phenotype only appears in the embryo, so clone screening must be genotype-only and the developmental cost is unseen until incubation.

results.title: A Step-by-Step Procedure for Producing Germline Chimera in Chicken via Primordial Germ Cell Transplantation (Choi, Han & Han 2025, J Vis Exp 226)
results.snippet: The operational protocol behind any claim of feasibility, from Jae Yong Han's lab (SNU). Gives the exact animal logistics a proposal must cost out: PGCs isolated from HH stage 26-28 embryos, cultured/expanded in vitro, then microinjected into the dorsal aorta of HH stage 14-17 recipient embryos; short-term engraftment tracked with PKH26, germline contribution confirmed by PCR of recipient gonads. Explicitly stated to be compatible with CRISPR/Cas9 and transposon vectors. Two things this makes concrete for the tail question: the whole pipeline runs through the same HH-staged window in which the avian tail bud is regressing, and the readout is a two-generation chimera-then-breed cycle, so 'one edited bird' means hundreds of incubated embryos — the numbers an animal-ethics committee actually reviews.

results.title: The ethics of reviving long extinct species (Sandler 2013, Conservation Biology 28:354-360)
results.snippet: The sharpest published articulation of the line between defensible evo-devo experiment and spectacle, and the closest peer-reviewed analogue to a 'dino-chicken' critique. Sandler's systematic conclusion is the load-bearing one: whatever reasons favour de-extinction 'do not have to do with its usefulness in species conservation; rather, they concern the status of revived species as scientific and technological achievements,' and it is 'ethically problematic to promote de-extinction as a significant conservation strategy.' He works through and partly grants the counter-arguments an atavism project faces head-on — animal suffering, unnaturalness, hubris, diversion of resources — and concludes such a project can be ethically acceptable only if welfare, ecological, legal and human-health concerns are 'thoroughly addressed.' Use this to frame the tail project honestly as a mechanistic hypothesis test, not a conservation or resurrection claim.

results.title: De-Extinction at a Crossroads: Ecology, Ethics, and the Future of Conservation in the Biotech Age (Paganeli & Galetti 2025, Ecology Letters 28:e70217; PMC12453136)
results.snippet: The current, post-dire-wolf version of the spectacle critique, and the most directly transferable warning for a 'dino-chicken' framing. Written after the 2025 Colossal announcement, it dissects exactly the failure mode at issue: an organism 'resembling' an extinct form, later clarified to be a modified grey wolf carrying a small fraction of dire wolf DNA, marketed as a revival. The authors' core argument — that de-extinction 'must not be guided by feasibility or commercial appeal alone' and needs a multidisciplinary framework covering invasion ecology, rewilding, ethics and governance — is the precedent for why a chicken with a few extra caudal vertebrae must not be presented as a dinosaur. Also useful as the honest-labelling standard: state what fraction of the phenotype and genotype is actually ancestral.

results.title: Generation of gene edited birds in one generation using sperm transfection assisted gene editing (STAGE) (Cooper et al. 2016, Transgenic Research 26:331-347)
results.snippet: A feasibility reality-check that keeps efficiency claims honest, and the main route for avian species where PGC culture does not exist. STAGE delivers CRISPR reagents via sperm to reach germline edits in a single generation rather than two, demonstrated by GFP knockout and by DMRT1 mutation in embryos and hatched chickens. The value here is the authors' own candour about variance: efficiency ranged 'from as low as 0% to as high as 26%', driven by gRNA efficiency and mRNA stability. Any in-silico design pipeline that outputs a single edit must therefore budget for a large embryo cohort and mosaic founders, and a power/animal-numbers justification for an ethics submission should use this range, not best-case figures. Caveat: DMRT1 editing produced embryos, and the paper is a single-lab method report whose efficiencies have not been broadly replicated.

results.title: Rashid et al. 2014, EvoDevo 5:25 — "From dinosaurs to birds: a tail of evolution"
results.snippet: The review explicitly requested. Its own abstract concedes the key point for this project: "virtually nothing is understood about the genetic and developmental events responsible for the emergence of short, fused tails." What it ACTUALLY does is not avian embryology — it is a curation of 23 MOUSE mutants that produce fused caudal vertebrae plus tail truncation, mostly in Notch/Wnt somite-boundary and differentiation genes, then correlates them to the fossil record (Archaeopteryx, Jeholornis, Sapeornis, Confuciusornis). So the mouse-to-bird transfer that the brief flags as the weak link is baked into the foundational review itself: the candidate gene list is a mouse-mutant catalogue, and the closing claim (that a small number of pleiotropic mutations could explain the sudden appearance of short-tailed birds) is stated as an "open question," i.e. proposed, not demonstrated. Open access (PMC4304130), 2014, cited ~22x — a thin citation base for a load-bearing review.

results.title: Rashid et al. 2018, Sci Rep 8:9014 — "Avian tail ontogeny, pygostyle formation, and interpretation of juvenile Mesozoic specimens"
results.snippet: The primary descriptive baseline for how the pygostyle actually forms in extant birds, and it overturns the naive embryonic model: fusion of distal caudal vertebrae into a pygostyle does NOT occur during embryogenesis at all — it happens post-hatching, near skeletal maturity, as does mineralization of vertebral processes. Also reports generation and then loss of intervertebral discs within the pygostyle, vertebral bodies derived from different cartilage types, and alternative modes of caudal process morphogenesis. Design consequence: the pygostyle is a post-embryonic ankylosis event, decoupled from the embryonic axial-elongation program — so an in-silico intervention on HH-stage elongation genes and an intervention on pygostyle fusion are two different targets, not one. Also shows the number of vertebrae incorporated into the pygostyle varies considerably across extant and Cretaceous birds, which weakens any fixed "N caudal somites" comparison to Archaeopteryx/Caudipteryx.

results.title: Miller & Briglin 1996, Dev Dyn 206:212-218 — "Apoptosis removes chick embryo tail gut and remnant of the primitive streak"
results.snippet: Directly answers the programmed-cell-death question, and the answer is largely NO for somites. TUNEL (ApopTag) across HH17-25 chick tail buds finds apoptosis concentrated in the median cell cord of the degenerating tail gut, in ventral tail-bud mesenchyme at older stages, in the primitive streak remnant (Hensen's node), and in postmembrane cloacal endoderm — but explicitly reports LACK of apoptosis markers in neural tube, notochord, and somites, supporting Schoenwolf's (1981) view that those tail-bud cells are assimilated into the growing rump rather than culled. The authors do interpret node-remnant apoptosis as "a stop signal for axial organization at the caudal terminus," which is the only PCD-based termination claim here and is an interpretation, not a perturbation result. Caveats to flag: single 1996 study, no replication found, descriptive TUNEL only, and it gives the HH17-25 window in which tail-bud remodelling occurs.

results.title: Rashid et al. 2020, Sci Rep 10:6303 — "Distal spinal nerve development and divergence of avian groups"
results.snippet: The best available Gallus-versus-Alligator comparative embryology on the caudal program. Defines the early developmental boundary between the proximal free-caudal region and the distal pygostyle domain in chicken, then tracks sclerotome anterior/posterior polarity and peripheral nervous system development from early embryo to post-hatching. Key results that complicate any single "avian tail program": the neognath pattern (spinal nerve development stopping at the pygostyle boundary) is NOT found in paleognathous emu, where spinal nerves extend through the pygostyle region; and the inferred ancestral long-tailed configuration, reconstructed from Anolis and Alligator mississippiensis, unexpectedly resembles neognaths more than paleognaths. Authors themselves raise an independently long-tailed paleognath ancestor as a possible scenario — explicitly hypothesis, not demonstration. Provides the alligator outgroup data the brief asks for, though as nerve/sclerotome pattern rather than caudal somite counts.

results.title: Rashid et al. 2023, PNAS 120:e2219757120 — "Nonpathological inflammation drives the development of an avian flight adaptation"
results.snippet: The mechanism paper for pygostyle fusion, and the only entry in this cluster with a causal perturbation rather than description. Transcriptome profiling plus immuno/histochemistry show that post-hatching vertebral fusion in the chicken tail runs through a sterile inflammatory response resembling bone fracture healing, implicating necroptosis, multiple immune cell types (notably heterophils) and previously unrecognized nucleus pulposus structures. Causal test: anti-inflammatory corticosteroid treatment INHIBITED vertebral fusion. For an in-silico reversal design this is the single most actionable finding on the pygostyle half of the phenotype — the fusion is an inflammation-dependent ankylosis process, druggable/perturbable postnatally, and therefore NOT a locus where a genomic language model scoring embryonic regulatory variants would have anything to say. Note the cell-death pathway implicated here is necroptosis in post-hatching bone, entirely separate from the embryonic tail-bud apoptosis question.

results.title: Rashid & Chapman 2021, Dev Dyn 250:1229-1235 — "The long and the short of tails"
results.snippet: Short perspective bridging embryonic to adult tail ontogeny across amniotes — mammals, birds, non-avian reptiles — covering mechanisms underlying tail length, neural systems, and tail regeneration. Useful mainly as the authors' own updated framing of what changed between the 2014 review and the 2018/2020 primary papers, and as a pointer to the comparative (squamate/crocodilian) literature for the outgroup baseline. It is a perspective, not data: treat every mechanistic statement in it as a signpost to a primary source rather than as evidence, and check whether each cited mechanism was established in mouse or actually tested in Gallus.

results.title: Rashid et al. 2014, EvoDevo — "From dinosaurs to birds: a tail of evolution" (PMID 25621146)
results.snippet: The target review itself. Critical for calibrating claim vs. speculation: the authors state outright that "virtually nothing is understood about the genetic and developmental events responsible for the emergence of short, fused tails" in birds. Their actual contribution is NOT avian experimental data — it is a curated survey of 23 MOUSE mutants whose pleiotropy couples fused caudal vertebrae (pygostyle-like) with tail truncation; at least half lie in the Notch/Wnt somite boundary-formation or differentiation pathway, altering somite number or size. The "few mutational events could explain the sudden fossil appearance of short-tailed birds" line is explicitly framed as an open question, not a result. So the mouse-to-bird transfer is not a weakness this paper accidentally has — it IS the paper's method, and nothing in it is a chick experiment.

results.title: Jurberg, Aires, Varela-Lasheras, Nóvoa & Mallo 2013, Dev Cell — "Switching axial progenitors from producing trunk to tail tissues in vertebrate embryos" (PMID 23763947)
results.snippet: The single most mechanistically load-bearing GDF11 paper for a tail-lengthening design. Shows in MOUSE that Gdf11 signaling coordinates the trunk-to-tail switch: loss of signaling delays the switch, premature activation shifts hindlimbs and cloaca up against the forelimbs and yields extremely short trunks. Mechanism has two arms — Gdf11 activates Isl1 to make hindlimb/cloacal lateral mesoderm, and it reallocates bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors from the anterior primitive streak into the tail bud, partly by reducing retinoic acid available to those progenitors. That ties GDF11 directly to the FGF/RA wavefront and to the NMP niche in one experiment. Flag: entirely mouse transgenics; no chick counterpart is presented, and the RA arm is inferential ("in part").

results.title: Robinton, Chal, ... Pourquié & Daley 2019, Dev Cell — "The Lin28/let-7 Pathway Regulates the Mammalian Caudal Body Axis Elongation Program" (PMID 30661985)
results.snippet: The primary source for the "Lin28a overexpression lengthens the mouse tail" claim, and the closest existing proof-of-concept for deliberately ADDING caudal vertebrae. FoxD1-driven Lin28a overexpression strikingly increased caudal vertebra number and tail-bud proliferation; Lin28a knockout did the reverse; let-7 manipulation gave opposite effects; LIN28B gave similar-but-distinct phenotypes. Proposed mechanism is heterochronic — prolonging the caudal progenitor pool and tilting the NMP neural/mesodermal balance toward mesoderm (Sox2 down). Flags: mouse only, one lab, not replicated in a non-mammal; and the pro-mesodermal Sox2 downregulation is precisely the axis along which the hominoid TBXT lesion trades tail length against neural tube integrity, so this is a mechanistic cost warning, not just a lever.

results.title: van de Ven, ... Mallo, Beck & Deschamps 2011, Development — "Concerted involvement of Cdx/Hox genes and Wnt signaling in morphogenesis of the caudal neural tube and cloacal derivatives from the posterior growth zone" (PMID 21752936)
results.snippet: Covers three of the requested modules in one genetic framework, all in MOUSE. (i) CDX dosage: an allelic series gives progressively more severe posterior vertebral defects as Cdx dose falls, and those defects are rescued by posterior gain-of-function of the Wnt effector Lef1 — placing Cdx upstream of canonical Wnt in the posterior growth zone. (ii) HOX13 as terminator: precocious expression of Hox paralogous-group 13 genes truncates the vertebral axis by antagonizing Cdx function. (iii) WNT3A: a novel Wnt3a hypomorph phenocopies the Cdx2/4 compound mutant. Important design constraint — all three genotypes also produce caudal neural tube dysmorphology including neural tube splitting, i.e. posterior axis extension and neural tube integrity are genetically coupled here too.

results.title: Economides, Zeltser & Capecchi 2003, Dev Biol — "Hoxb13 mutations cause overgrowth of caudal spinal cord and tail vertebrae" (PMID 12679105)
results.snippet: Primary source for the Hoxb13-null longer-tail phenotype. Homozygous loss-of-function mice show overgrowth of ALL major tail-bud derivatives — secondary neural tube, caudal spinal ganglia, and caudal vertebrae — traced to increased proliferation plus DECREASED apoptosis within the tail. Reads Hoxb13 as an activator of apoptotic pathways in the secondary neural tube and a general repressor of caudal vertebral growth, i.e. a genuine terminator of axial extension rather than a patterning gene. Directly relevant to the "is the avian distal tail eliminated by programmed cell death" question, but note the apoptosis evidence here is mouse; nothing in this paper is avian, and the HOX13 paralog whose loss lengthens the tail is B13 specifically, not the A/C/D13 paralogs.

results.title: Gamer, Cox, Small & Rosen 2001, Dev Biol — "Gdf11 is a negative regulator of chondrogenesis and myogenesis in the developing chick limb" (PMID 11203700)
results.snippet: Included specifically because it is one of the very few papers that carries GDF11 across the mouse/chick boundary with actual chick experiments — and it shows the transfer is not clean. Chicken Gdf11 was cloned and is expressed in distal limb mesoderm; GDF11 protein beads in the wing bud caused severe truncation of cartilage and muscle and induced ectopic Hoxd-11 and Hoxd-13 (but not Hoxa-11/a-13/Msx). The paper's framing device is the dichotomy it names: Gdf11-null MICE show anterior homeotic transformations of the axial skeleton (from McPherron, Lawler & Lee 1999, Nat Genet, https://doi.org/10.1038/10320 — Gdf11 expressed in primitive streak, presomitic mesoderm and tail bud; dose-dependent, Gdf11+/- milder than -/-; Hox expression shifted, so Gdf11 acts upstream of Hox) yet the limb is unaffected in those same knockouts. Conclusion for the design: for GDF11 the chick evidence is limb, pharmacological (bead), and gain-of-function — there is no published chick axial/tail-bud Gdf11 loss-of-function, so the axial role in birds is assumed, not demonstrated.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-assisted homologous recombination can produce precise, targeted knock-ins at a defined locus in cultured chicken primordial germ cells with essentially complete accuracy among drug-selected clones — establishing that site-directed germline knock-in (not just indel knockout) is technically available in Gallus gallus, which is the wet-lab prerequisite for any proposed regulatory-element edit in an avian atavism experiment.
claims.quote: All of the resulting drug-resistant clones contained the correct targeting event.

claims.claim: Edited chicken PGCs went through the germline and produced live, genotype-confirmed edited offspring: 46 EGFP-positive progeny from one edited PGC line were hatched and all carried the intended targeted insertion — i.e. germline-transgenic galliformes derived from edited PGCs are a demonstrated, not hypothetical, outcome.
claims.quote: Forty-six EGFP-positive progeny from transmission of cell line 1783–10 were hatched and typed for the CRISPR-targeted IgH KO6B. All of the EGFP-positive birds contained the IgH KO6B insertion.

claims.claim: Germline transmission efficiency of edited PGC lines is highly variable and unreliable per line, ranging from zero transmission to near-complete transmission across different cell lines — so the practical bottleneck in chicken germline editing is chimera transmission, not the edit itself, and any project plan must budget for screening multiple PGC lines.
claims.quote: one chimera with close to 100% transmission of the injected cells

claims.claim: Without drug selection, the homologous-recombination targeting efficiency in chicken PGCs is far below 100% — reported as roughly 20–25% at worst for the less efficient gRNAs — meaning this 2016 protocol depends on an integrated selection cassette, which is a design constraint for a 'clean' regulatory edit intended to model an ancestral allele.
claims.quote: the targeting efficiency was, at worst, 20–25%

claims.claim: The study did not assay off-target mutagenesis, so the phenotypes of the resulting germline-edited birds cannot be causally attributed to the intended edit alone — a caveat that applies directly to any future claim that an engineered avian phenotype (e.g. an extended caudal axis) results from a specific designed lesion.
claims.quote: we did not test for off-target mutations and thus cannot rule out mutations that could lead to more specific phenotypes in these birds or to effects in future generations

claims.claim: Colossal's 2025 "dire wolf" was produced by CRISPR-Cas9 editing of ~20 loci across 14 genes in a grey wolf genome, i.e. a genetically modified extant proxy carrying a tiny proportion of extinct-species DNA rather than a restored species — the same logical status any "dino-chicken"/avian-atavism construct would have.
claims.quote: Colossal Laboratories, in its efforts to recreate certain traits of the extinct dire wolf, sequenced DNA and used CRISPR-Cas9 techniques to edit approximately 20 key available genetic differences (loci) into 14 genes of modern grey wolves." ... "In early 2025, a genetically engineered organism resembling the dire wolf was announced as de-extinct, though it was later clarified to be a modified grey wolf containing only a tiny proportion of dire wolf DNA.

claims.claim: Peer-reviewed conservation biologists explicitly charge that flagship genome-editing "de-extinction" projects may be motivated by demonstrating technological feasibility and attracting wealthy donors rather than by research value — the published spectacle critique the research question asks for, applied to the closest analogue of an avian atavism project.
claims.quote: It remains unclear whether the aim is to use those organisms for research or simply to showcase technological feasibility and bring attention from wealthy donors.

claims.claim: The authors propose that de-extinction-type germline engineering should be governed by ecological risk assessment plus ethical review modelled on biomedical research review, not by existing conservation or agricultural animal frameworks — i.e. as of Sept 2025 no dedicated review pathway exists and one is being argued for.
claims.quote: This includes thorough ecological risk assessments, ethical reviews akin to those in biomedical research, inclusive public engagement, and prioritisation of funding for protecting existing biodiversity." ... "Animal welfare is another major concern. As we previously mentioned, what are the rights and well-being of organisms created in laboratories, especially if they are destined for containment or experimental use?

claims.claim: The paper names a specific moral-hazard mechanism — "extinction offsetting" — as the main ethical cost of de-extinction framing, and argues the opportunity cost is the decisive objection ("every dollar spent resurrecting the past is a dollar not spent to protect the present").
claims.quote: If extinction is seen as temporary or easily reversible, it may encourage complacency—or worse, justify ecologically unsustainable actions under the illusion that any damage can later be undone. This mindset of 'extinction offsetting' threatens to replace the moral and scientific foundations upon which conservation has long been built.

claims.claim: Birds are named as active engineering targets (giant moa Dinornis spp., dodo Raphus cucullatus) but this source supplies no avian-specific technical content — nothing on primordial germ cells, germline chimeras, galliform transgenesis, atavism, or axial/tail development. It is an ethics/policy source only and cannot support any mechanistic claim about the avian tail program.
claims.quote: the company appears to aim for this trait, as shown by its plans to de-extinct other large-bodied species, such as the woolly mammoth and the giant moa (Dinornis spp.), a 3-m-tall, 250-kg bird once native to New Zealand.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas9 editing in cultured chicken primordial germ cells (PGCs) reaches >90% efficiency at the ovalbumin (OVA) and ovomucoid (OVM) loci, and targeted knock-in at the CVH (chicken vasa homolog) locus reaches 82% efficiency — i.e. the PGC route gives high-efficiency, site-specific germline editing in Gallus gallus, not just somatic editing.
claims.quote: over 90% editing efficiency when targeting the ovalbumin and ovomucoid genes in cultured PGCs ... achieving dual fluorescent knock-in at the CVH locus with 82% efficiency

claims.claim: Cultured chicken PGCs can be expanded long-term on STO/BRL feeders (or feeder-free) in knockout DMEM with SCF and FGF, injected into recipient embryos, and yield germline chimeras with transmission demonstrated through three progeny generations, with a reported ~6% chimeric-male rate from PGC-like cells — establishing the full culture-to-germline pipeline needed for any multi-step developmental edit in chicken.

claims.claim: Base editing is measurably less efficient in avian PGCs than in avian somatic cells, attributed to high expression of base-excision-repair genes; chicken codon optimization of the editor improved efficiency by only ~10.4%. Prime editing in chicken exists only as a single proof-of-concept (reporter correction plus a stop codon in endogenous DDX4), so precise single-nucleotide regulatory edits in chicken germline are far less mature than knockout-scale CRISPR.
claims.quote: base editing is less efficient in avian PGCs than in somatic cells, likely due to high expression of base excision repair (BER) genes

claims.claim: Chicken PGC culture protocols are species-specific and not transferable across birds — goose PGC self-renewal requires BMP4 and is inhibited by Activin A, the inverse of the chicken requirement — which bounds any claim that a chicken-validated germline pipeline generalizes to other galliformes or to non-model birds.
claims.quote: The culture protocols optimized for chickens are not universally applicable. A striking example is found in the goose, where PGC self-renewal is dependent on BMP4 and is actively inhibited by Activin A—the exact opposite of the core requirement in chickens

claims.claim: Practical constraints on the chicken PGC pipeline are quantified: cryopreservation drops survival to ~46.5% with reduced functional capacity, apoptosis limits cell yield, and prolonged culture (the prerequisite for multi-step editing) accumulates genetic and epigenetic aberrations — directly relevant to a multi-locus axial/caudal program edit requiring many sequential rounds.

results.title: Comprehensive review and assessment of multi-species splicing variant prediction: task-specific deep learning models and genomic foundation models (Sun et al., Brief Bioinform 2026; PMID 42323878)
results.snippet: The single most directly on-point source for this angle, and apparently the only published benchmark that explicitly includes CHICKEN in a genomic-foundation-model variant-effect evaluation. Benchmarks 10 models (4 task-specific DL + 6 GFMs including DNABERT-2 and Evo 2) on human, rat, pig and chicken splicing-variant datasets. Key numbers: task-specific human-trained models lose ~21-33% AUROC when transferred to non-human species; adding a lightweight MLP on FROZEN GFM embeddings recovers much of that (8.56-23.84% residual decline for rat/pig), and chicken performance came within 1% of human — 'even exceeding by 0.52% when using the Evo 2 embedding'. Three heavy caveats for the parent question: (a) the task is SPLICING variant effect, not enhancer/cis-regulatory effect, so it does not license using Evo 2 for avian regulatory predictions; (b) it is a single non-replicated benchmark on 'manually assembled' datasets; (c) Nucleotide Transformer and Caduceus are not among the models where chicken results are reported. Retrieved via PubMed.

results.title: An atlas of regulatory elements in chicken: a resource for chicken genetics and genomics (Pan et al., Sci Adv 2023, 9:eade1204; PMID 37134160)
results.snippet: The reference chicken cis-regulatory resource any enhancer-level analysis of the caudal/axial program would have to be built on. Integrates 377 genome-wide sequencing datasets across 23 ADULT tissues to annotate 1.57 million regulatory elements in 15 chromatin states, ~1.2 million predicted enhancer-gene pairs and 7,662 super-enhancers. Critical limitation for a tail-development question: the tissue panel is adult, so it contains NO tailbud, presomitic mesoderm or neuromesodermal-progenitor chromatin — the exact cell states where an axial-termination enhancer would be active. Also a coordinate-version trap: the annotation is tied to the assembly used in 2023 (GRCg6a-era galGal6 lineage), so any interval lifted from it must be re-lifted before being compared to GRCg7b/T2T coordinates. Retrieved via PubMed.

results.title: The ChickenGTEx portal: a pan-tissue catalogue of regulatory variants shaping transcriptomic and phenotypic diversity (Hou et al., Nucleic Acids Res 2026, 54:D982-D993; PMID 40827640)
results.snippet: The closest thing to a chicken equivalent of human GTEx, and therefore the only avian dataset that could ground-truth a regulatory-variant-effect prediction. Contains ~2.2 million molQTL with 806,229 fine-mapped, 1,956 context-dependent molQTL, 257 epigenomic profiles (7 marks, 15 chromatin states) across 23 tissues, and 185,376 single-cell expression profiles across 191 cell clusters from 9 tissues, from a 2,869-chicken / 123-breed imputation panel. This is the validation substrate a model like Evo 2 or Nucleotide Transformer would have to be scored against for avian regulatory prediction — and no such scoring appears to be published. Same caveat as the atlas: it is a breed/production-trait resource built on adult tissues, giving no embryonic tailbud coverage, and its coordinates are assembly-pinned. Retrieved via PubMed.

results.title: Near telomere-to-telomere genome assemblies of Silkie Gallus gallus and Mallard Anas platyrhynchos restored the structure of chromosomes and 'missing' genes in birds (Zhao et al., J Anim Sci Biotechnol 2025, 16:9; PMID 39828703)
results.snippet: The assembly-version caveat in its strongest form, and it bears directly on question (4) 'is avian tail reduction gene loss or regulation?'. The authors recovered 325 genes previously scored as MISSING in birds purely by improving the assembly (GC-rich microchromosomes and heterochromatic regions were the culprits), and annotated TNFA in mallard for the first time. Practical consequence: any claim that a gene in the axial/caudal program is absent or pseudogenized in the avian lineage must be re-checked against a near-T2T assembly before being believed — historical 'avian gene loss' lists are contaminated by assembly gaps. Also means that every coordinate-level statement about a chicken locus needs its assembly version (galGal6/GRCg6a vs GRCg7b vs these T2T assemblies) stated explicitly. Retrieved via PubMed.

results.title: Conservation of cis-regulatory codes over half a billion years of evolution (Ogawa et al., Sci Adv 2025, 11:eadw7681; PMID 41385645)
results.snippet: The best available empirical evidence on whether regulatory logic learned in one vertebrate lineage transfers to birds — the crux of the mouse-to-chicken transfer problem flagged in the question. Single-cell chromatin accessibility across lamprey, fish, BIRD and mammal retina shows the cis-regulatory CODE (clustering of high-affinity TF binding sites in cell-class-specific open chromatin) is conserved despite extensive turnover of the cis-regulatory REGIONS themselves. The useful methodological reading for an atavism project: sequence-level orthology of enhancers between mouse and chicken should not be expected, so an alignment-based hunt for a 'mouse axial-termination enhancer' in chicken is likely to fail even where the underlying regulatory logic is conserved — motif/code-level comparison is the defensible approach. Caveat: the evidence is from retina, a single organ system, not axial mesoderm. Retrieved via PubMed.

results.title: Genome Editing in the Chicken: From PGC-Mediated Germline Transmission to Advanced Applications (He et al., Int J Mol Sci 2025, 26:9426; PMID 41096693)
results.snippet: Review covering the wet-lab feasibility half of the in-silico-to-experiment chain: why avian genome editing lagged mammals (no pronuclear injection possible given avian reproductive biology), and how in vitro culture of primordial germ cells made chicken a tractable germline-editing model, through to modern CRISPR-based systems, disease-resistance engineering, surrogate hosts and oviduct bioreactors. Relevant as the reality check on any predicted regulatory edit: the established route is PGC culture plus germline chimera production, which constrains what kind of lesion (knockout vs precise regulatory base edit) is actually deliverable. Companion primary/protocol sources found in the same search: Choi et al. JoVE 2025 step-by-step PGC transplantation protocol (doi:10.3791/69704, HH26-28 donor, HH14-17 recipient dorsal aorta) and Kang et al. Anim Biosci 2023 Z-chromosome GFP knockin via PGCs (doi:10.5713/ab.22.0405). Retrieved via PubMed.

Any avian germline-modification design must be built around these two HH windows.

claims.quote: Traditional approaches using blastodermal cells from EGK stage X embryos are limited by low germline transmission efficiency due to early cell lineage segregation. In contrast, PGC-mediated strategies exploit the intrinsic germline competency of these unipotent cells, enabling reliable incorporation into recipient gonads.

results.title: Lovell et al. 2014, Genome Biology — Conserved syntenic clusters of protein coding genes are missing in birds (PMID 25518852, PMC4290089)
results.snippet: The reference catalogue of avian gene loss: ~274 protein-coding genes present in most vertebrates are absent across 60 bird genomes, mostly in syntenic clusters at chromosomal-rearrangement breakpoints, and still present in crocodilians — i.e. lost on the avian stem after the split from Crocodylia, exactly the branch of interest. DECISIVE NULL FOR THE TAIL: I fetched the full text and searched it for HOX/HOXA13/HOXB13/HOXD13, CDX1/2/4, TBXT/Brachyury, GDF11, LIN28A/LIN28B, WNT3A, FGF8, ALDH1A2, CYP26A1 and for 'somite', 'tail', 'caudal', 'axial' — none appear. The avian axial-elongation/termination program is not in the missing-gene set. This separates tail from teeth: teeth have hard pseudogenization evidence (ENAM, AMEL, AMBN, DSPP), the tail has none. Caveat: the study predates the B10K/VGP high-quality assemblies and is alignment/annotation-based on 2014-era draft genomes, so absence-of-evidence for any single gene is assembly-dependent — the claim to make is 'no published gene loss linked to the axial program', not 'proven no gene loss'.

results.title: Seki et al. 2017, Nature Communications — Functional roles of Aves class-specific cis-regulatory elements on macroevolution of bird-specific features (PMID 28165450)
results.snippet: The positive counterpart to the gene-loss null: across 48 bird genomes the authors identify millions of avian-specific highly conserved elements (ASHCEs), >99% non-coding, with differential histone marks in developing limb, and functionally demonstrate one ASHCE driving avian-specific Sim1 expression tied to flight-feather development. Establishes that the dinosaur-to-bird transition is documented at the level of cis-regulatory rewiring and avian-specific conserved non-coding elements, not gene loss. NOTE: the ASHCE analysis is limb/feather-focused; I found no ASHCE claim about caudal somites, the tailbud, or Hox/CDX/TBXT/GDF11 axial termination, so this supports 'regulation is the right class of hypothesis for the tail' by analogy only, not by direct evidence.

results.title: Sackton et al. 2019, Science — Convergent regulatory evolution and loss of flight in paleognathous birds (PMID 30948549)
results.snippet: The strongest in-clade precedent that avian morphological LOSS is regulatory rather than coding. 11 new palaeognath genomes (including an extinct moa); Bayesian analysis of 284,001 conserved non-coding elements — 60,665 corroborated as enhancers by developmental ATAC/open-chromatin — finds 2,355 independent accelerations along flightless lineages, with enhancer-reporter functional consequences in the developing forelimb, while convergent protein-coding change is comparatively absent. Directly transferable method for the tail question: CNEE acceleration testing on the avian stem branch for axial/caudal genes. Caveat: this is repeated loss within crown birds (many independent flightless lineages give statistical power); the tail was lost ONCE on a single stem branch, so the convergence-based test that worked here has no replicate branches and is not directly applicable — a real design constraint to flag.

results.title: Shakya et al. 2025, BMC Biology — Convergent evolution of noncoding elements associated with short tarsus length in birds (PMID 39984930)
results.snippet: Most recent and most directly analogous published test: an avian SKELETAL-REDUCTION phenotype dissected with comparative genomics. Uses a new, openly available set of 932,467 avian conserved non-exonic elements (CNEEs) over a 79-bird whole-genome alignment; finds convergent acceleration in 14,422 elements in short-tarsus clades, enriched near skeletal-system-development genes, while 9,854 protein-coding genes show NO convergent positive selection. Same verdict as Sackton: regulatory, not coding. Practically, the 932k-CNEE set plus the 79-genome alignment are the concrete resource to reuse if you want to ask the same question of caudal/axial genes. Same single-branch limitation applies to the tail.

results.title: Rashid et al. 2014, EvoDevo — From dinosaurs to birds: a tail of evolution (PMID 25621146)
results.snippet: The review the brief names, and it answers the gene-loss-vs-regulation question by default: it states outright that 'virtually nothing is understood about the genetic and developmental events responsible for the emergence of short, fused tails'. Its candidate list is NOT derived from avian comparative genomics — it is reverse-engineered from a curated set of MOUSE mutants, 23 of which give fused caudal vertebrae plus tail truncation, at least half in Notch/Wnt somite-boundary formation or differentiation, correlated post hoc to the fossil record. So the entire candidate-gene framework for the avian tail rests on mouse-to-bird extrapolation and is explicitly speculative, not on any observed avian gene loss, pseudogene, or CNE loss. Flag: this is a review, not primary evidence, and its candidate list should be cited as hypotheses generated from mouse, never as avian findings.

results.title: Hintermann et al. 2022, Development — Developmental and evolutionary comparative analysis of a regulatory landscape in mouse and chicken (PMID 35770682)
results.snippet: Quantifies the mouse-to-bird weak link at the exact locus that matters. Compares Hoxd regulatory landscapes between mouse and chicken, including regulation during elongation of the POSTERIOR TRUNK (not just skin appendages): the amniote chromatin topology is ancestral and the trunk-elongation CREs are partly conserved in position, but a high proportion of the non-coding sequences active in the trunk have FUNCTIONALLY DIVERGED between mouse and chicken — transcriptional output is robust while enhancer sequence is not. Consequence for the project: a mouse posterior-Hox enhancer cannot be assumed to be the orthologous chicken enhancer, so any Evo 2 / NT / DNABERT variant-effect call transferred from mouse coordinates to galGal/bGalGal is unsupported by sequence homology alone. Also implies conserved-CNE-loss scans will be noisy in this landscape because functional turnover happens without sequence loss.

claims.claim: In the chick tail bud, apoptosis markers are ABSENT from neural tube, notochord and somites — i.e. the paper provides direct negative evidence that caudal somites/axial tissues are NOT eliminated by programmed cell death; instead it supports Schoenwolf (1981)'s model that these cells are assimilated into the growing rump. This is the single most load-bearing claim for the 'are distal caudal somites deleted by PCD in birds?' question, and the answer from this primary source is no for somites (PCD is restricted to tail gut, streak remnant and ventral mesenchyme). Retrieved via PubMed (PMID 8725288); Wiley full text returned HTTP 403, so the claim rests on the published abstract, and the study is a single descriptive, non-replicated correlative survey.
claims.quote: Lack of apoptosis markers in neural tube, notochord, and somites supports the suggestion of Schoenwolf ([1981] Anat, Embryol. (Beri.) 162:183-197) that cells of those areas in the tail bud are assimilated into the growing rump of the chick embryo.

claims.claim: Cells of the remnant of the primitive streak (Hensen's node) in the chick tail bud are apoptotic, and the authors interpret this as programmed cell death acting as a 'stop signal' for axial organization at the caudal terminus — a candidate cell-biological terminator of avian axial elongation. Note this is an interpretive suggestion from TUNEL/ApopTag staining patterns, not a functional test (no gene perturbation, no rescue), and no molecular pathway (GDF11, HOX13, CDX, LIN28/let-7, TBXT) is implicated by this study.
claims.quote: Cells of the remnant of the primitive streak (Hensen's node) mark for apoptosis, suggesting that programmed cell death is a stop signal for axial organization at the caudal terminus.

claims.claim: The apoptosis survey was performed on Gallus gallus embryos across Hamburger-Hamilton stages HH17-25 using ApopTag (TUNEL-type) with peroxidase/diaminobenzidine detection, which fixes the HH window in which avian tail-bud cell death and terminal axial events are documented by this source.
claims.quote: We used ApopTagTM (Oncor, Gaithersburg, MD) with the peroxidase/diaminobenzidine (DAB) procedure to correlate apoptosis with earlier reports of patterns of cell death in stage HH17-25 embryos, and our results suggest that the cell death inferred with supravital staining and appearance of cells in morphogenesis of the tail bud is programmed cell death called apoptosis.

claims.claim: Where apoptosis does occur in the chick tail bud it is spatially restricted: most abundant in the median cell cord of the occluded, degenerating tail gut, and in tail-bud mesenchyme most frequently in the ventrum of older stages — i.e. the dying structures are transient endodermal/mesenchymal features, not the segmented paraxial mesoderm that would form caudal vertebrae.
claims.quote: Apoptosis markers in tail bud are most abundant in the median cell cord of occluded degenerating tail gut. Tail bud mesenchyme marks for apoptosis most frequently in the ventrum of older stages, where cell death has been reported.

claims.claim: Apoptosis is not implicated in cavitation of the medullary cord during chick secondary neurulation, but the authors explicitly flag this negative as provisional — an author-declared limitation that should be carried forward rather than cited as settled.
claims.quote: Lack of markers in neural tube of tail bud formed by secondary neurulation suggests that apoptosis is not involved in cavitation of medullary cord, but further investigation is necessary.

claims.claim: Sandler's ethical analysis concludes that the reasons favoring de-extinction are NOT conservation reasons but rest on the revived organism's status as a scientific/technological achievement — i.e. the field's own ethics literature already locates the value of such projects in demonstration rather than conservation benefit. This is the peer-reviewed anchor for the 'spectacle vs. scientific value' critique that applies directly to a 'dino-chicken' / avian atavism program, which likewise produces no conservation good and must be justified on knowledge-generation grounds alone. NOTE: only the publisher abstract was accessible (Wiley full text 403, not in PMC), so the supporting argumentation in the body is not verified here.
claims.quote: the reasons in favor of pursuing de-extinction do not have to do with its usefulness in species conservation; rather, they concern the status of revived species as scientific and technological achievements

claims.claim: Sandler argues it is ethically problematic to PROMOTE de-extinction as a significant conservation strategy, on three stated grounds: it does not prevent extinctions, does not address the causes of extinction, and could be detrimental to some conservation efforts (the moral-hazard / diverted-resources argument). Applied to an avian tail-atavism project, this means any framing of the work as conservation-relevant or as 'bringing back dinosaurs' is, per this source, an illegitimate justification.
claims.quote: it would be ethically problematic to promote de-extinction as a significant conservation strategy, because it does not prevent species extinctions, does not address the causes of extinction, and could be detrimental to some species conservation efforts

claims.claim: Sandler explicitly denies any human obligation or responsibility to pursue de-extinction of long-extinct species and states that reviving them addresses no urgent problem — placing the entire burden of justification on the proponent. For a tail-reversion experiment this means the design constraint is not 'is it permitted?' but 'does the knowledge gained outweigh the welfare cost?', with no countervailing duty to act.
claims.quote: humanity does not have a responsibility or obligation to pursue de-extinction of long extinct species, and reviving them does not address any urgent problem

claims.claim: Animal suffering is one of the four counter-arguments Sandler formally assesses (alongside unnaturalness, ecological/human-health harm, and hubris), and he sets a conjunctive acceptability condition: animal-welfare concerns must be THOROUGHLY ADDRESSED for a de-extinction to be ethically acceptable. This supplies the published standard against which the known welfare cost of a TBXT-type axial manipulation (neural tube defects in the Xia et al. 2024 mouse model) would have to be weighed in an avian germline experiment.
claims.quote: legitimate ecological, political, animal welfare, legal, or human health concerns associated with a de-extinction (and reintroduction) must be thoroughly addressed for it to be ethically acceptable

claims.claim: SCOPE LIMITATION / transfer caveat: the paper's object is the revival of species extinct for 'decades, centuries, or even millennia' via a cloning-type pathway (MeSH: Cloning, Biotechnology, Extinction), not the engineered re-expression of an ancestral trait in an extant species. Sandler's conclusions therefore apply to an avian atavism program only by analogy — the framing critique transfers cleanly, but the ecological-release and reintroduction analyses do not, since an atavistic chicken embryo is never reintroduced to a habitat.
claims.quote: There now appears to be a plausible pathway for reviving species that have been extinct for several decades, centuries, or even millennia. I conducted an ethical analysis of de-extinction of long extinct species.
